#2822. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

Fake comeback attempt by New York on Friday.

Fake concerning development across the nation's airspace, too.

Here's a bunch of the latest, including some interesting Josh Hart revelations.

On the decision to draw up the final shot for Karl-Anthony Towns instead of Jalen Brunson:

"We needed a 2-pointer. We had executed something like that in practice. We thought we would gain an advantage with a little rip screen. KAT got a great look. Probably a shot that he makes nine out of 10 times. So I'm okay with it."

On what really led to the Knicks' loss to Indiana:

"That play was something we liked, and we went to it. But I'll say this: That play did not cost us the game. We were lucky a little bit, and our guys did fight to give us a chance down the stretch. But I don't care who you play, it's going to be hard to win a game on the road when you lose the possession game like we did, if we get blown by on defense as bad as we did, if you let your opponent win the physicality battle like we did. It's all a recipe for a loss. And that's where I'm disappointed."

"I don't know if we fouled that much, but we were fouling. They just could keep putting their head down and driving into us, and we weren't ready to play. We didn't do our work early and get in the stance, being ready to guard these guys off the dribble drive, and they just walked to the free-throw line time after time after time."

On his reaction to the no-call on OG Anunoby's drive to the basket:

"I did get a T, but the reality of it is they were playing harder than us. It was out of frustration. Some of it because we just had a game that we played, and you have a guy like Jalen [Brunson] who's an All-Star and an MVP candidate; he goes 0-0 from the free-throw line. And at the end of the first half [here], I think it was maybe 20 to three or something like that, and that in itself is frustrating.

"To know that we're getting beat that bad from the free-throw line, and they're missing some calls. Now, are we fouling? Yes, and we got to do a better job doing our work earlier. But in the same breath, the discrepancy shouldn't be that bad two games in a row. Hopefully not three games in a row coming up.

"And that's what I'm taking a look at. That there are some fouls that they're calling with our body because guys are just putting their head down and running into you and snapping their head back, but we're not getting those same calls, and that is the frustrating part."

On the Knicks' inconsistent offensive rhythm and the need to improve:

"No, not yet. Not yet. At times, yes, but we're not always in a good flow right now, which is fine, because there are other ways to win a basketball game while we're trying to work on that."

On missing the potential game-tying shot against Indiana:

"I thought it was a great shot. I was excited for the opportunity. I got to make a quick decision. It's either OG is open on the rip screen and he has an open layup or I get to take the shot. I just was ready for the opportunity. … I'm happy with the follow through. I was happy with the technique. It just wasn't my day."

On taking full responsibility for his struggles and needing to improve:

"I just look in the mirror, I just got to be better. Nobody else to blame but me and I just got to go out there and, whatever it is, just be better and go harder.

"When times are tough, you just gotta own up to it and just be better.

"I try to be my best throughout the whole year. Obviously, struggles come, which obviously nobody wants, but like I said, in these moments, gotta look in the mirror and you're tested the most and just see what you're made of. So, just gotta be better.

On the Knicks' crowded wing rotation and the possibility of roster changes:

"There are several different ways you can look at it. You can look at it, if [Shamet and McBride] have it going, cool. Good. You could look at it like, 'Okay, maybe something else has to change [like a trade].'

"But there's going to good days with that, bad days. But whatever allows the Knicks the best opportunity and chance to win, that's the most important."

On the Knicks' slow pace limiting the effectiveness of Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby:

"There's less chances at the rim. I think it also affects Mikal and OG. … [Coach Mike Brown] says Mikal is the best runner in the league. So if you have the best runner in the league and you're not running, you're wasting one of his talents. If we play faster, we'll be able to do that. Sometimes OG has smaller guards defending him, so if we run he can be able to seal at the rim, be able to get easy points at the rim, which also can help our rim finishing."

On speeding up the Knicks' offense even if Jalen Brunson doesn't bring the ball up the court:

"We gotta get the ball out and sometimes that might have to be [Brunson] just running and not going to the ball after a make or a defensive rebound. Just trying to get a better and quicker flow so it's not so stagnant in the halfcourt."

On how his calf and ankle injuries disrupted his conditioning and preparation for the season:

"This year was a little different. Obviously, a shorter break in terms of the summer [because of the long playoff run] but also I wasn't physically able to really push my body towards the end of the summer to be prepared for the season. I had [the calf] injury in September, which kept me out for about three weeks, so I wasn't able to get in some of that conditioning and some of those legs under me, which is normally the time to do it.

"And then, the ankle injury in training camp. So, the ramp up was a little bit slower than I kinda wanted it to be or kinda liked it to be, so I think that's the biggest thing is just getting my legs under me."

On his shooting struggles and the impact of missing several weeks of basketball activity:

"The shots I'm shooting, I like them. I think that was kinda evident with Cleveland. One of the things: All three of my 3s was just hella short. It was just, those legs, get those legs under me.

"Also, on top of that, missing a week in the season, it's cumulative of six, seven weeks of just not much activity basketball-wise. So, I think that's just what it is. So, as the season progresses and I'm out there running more, doing all those kinds of things, the performance will follow."

On his mental struggles following the loss to Indiana:

"Just have to be better. Have to be better mentally. I just gotta get my mental right."

On not knowing how to improve his mental state and on-court performance:

"Wish I could tell you. Don't know. … I gotta figure out how to improve that and improve my play."

On why he has struggled to finish shots around the rim:

"It's early. We're not where we wanna be, but it's November. Everything needs to be better."

On the need for staying ready and responding to adversity:

"You're playing well one day and [then] next time you get punched in the mouth. So it's always about how you respond in this league."

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 1:30 p.m. EST Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.

By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services.

In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks.

The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.

For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16.

The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding.

When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed.

Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks.

#2815. Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.

Nondescript lots holding idle bulldozers, trucks and other industrial equipment are a common sight in local real estate markets across the U.S., and increasingly, a focus for Wall Street private investment giants.

If you haven't noticed them, it's probably because they so easily fade into the landscape, just another non-branded bit of land in the miasma of suburbia. But Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world's largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls industrial outdoor storage, or IOS. Investors are eyeing these lots as the AI build-out increases the demand for heavy equipment.

"We have strong conviction in industrial outdoor storage, which plays a critical role in our supply chain," said Devin Barnwell, a managing partner and co-leader of Brookfield's logistics business.

He says that up until now, the segment has been fragmented, but Brookfield sees that changing.

"We see significant opportunity to bring institutional capital and operating expertise to this fragmented sector, improving the quality and efficiency of these assets while strengthening the resilience of our industrial supply chains," Barnwell said.

Brookfield spent $1.2 billion earlier this year to take Peakstone Realty Trust private, a deal completed in May that gave it a portfolio of more than 70 industrial properties, most of them outdoor storage yards.

Blackstone is also ramping up in the sector, mainly as a lender. Its real estate debt arm has made six loans to outdoor storage owners totaling more than $1.1 billion, including a $244 million loan in June to Alterra IOS to buy 37 properties.

Despite the billions being bet on the market by Wall Street, there is still opportunity in the market for individual investors and local entrepreneurs looking to park their money where others park their equipment.

"1,000 percent yes," said Adam Petrillo, an executive managing director at Newmark, a commercial real estate advisory firm, who co-leads its industrial outdoor storage practice.

Petrillo said smaller, non-institutional investors, still control a significant amount of well-placed storage in secondary markets. "The good news for smaller investors and mom and pops is that a good individual IOS site isn't necessarily 50 acres," Petrillo said.

Lots as small as three to five acres in primary or secondary markets can still yield a robust return, he said.  "At that bite size, an individual can step in. We are not talking about tens of millions ... a three-acre, well-located IOS with multiple use cases can be found, marketed, leased,  and stabilized," he added.

Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses.

Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically.

The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial.

Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025.

Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said.

Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots.

"It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added.

Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors.

"Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said.

Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said.

"Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added.

"If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said.

CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future.

Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields.

"Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said.

For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added.

Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS.

Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants.

And institutional money is making IOS more competitive.

"Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said.

He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said.

For local investors, that means there is the ability to build a portfolio at a smaller scale and hold the assets for cash flow, or aggregate more than $10 million in assets and seek a portfolio premium when selling to institutional capital.

But buyers need to understand what they are getting into. Due diligence on tenant demand by site and site function, and tenant turnover ratio, are important factors in buying the right asset. Market diversity can also provide protection, Sutterer said.

"In Chicago, no single user category accounts for more than 18% of IOS tenants, helping insulate the market from industry-specific slowdowns," he said. Tenants' tendency to stay and tight vacancy rates nationally are current advantages of the asset class. In Chicagoland, for example, vacancy is below 3%.

Still, all the due diligence in the world can't protect investors from some variables.

"No one outside the Federal Reserve can control the cost of debt," said Kellie McIvor, vice president of acquisitions at Redwood Living, an Ohio real estate development firm. She said that right now, the cost of debt for light industrial uses is lower than, say, for residential construction.

"However, interest rates are still high, with no relief in sight," McIvor said.

The Fed is expected to raise rates in December in its effort to tame inflation, and after this week's latest hot October CPI report, potentially hike twice more in early 2027, according to some Wall Street forecasts.

"Because lenders view them as riskier than a large institutional investor, smaller buyers can face more expensive debt and may be asked to bring more equity to the deal. That can make financing a small acquisition disproportionately expensive. ... More expensive debt means less room for error in execution," McIvor said.

A small buyer looking at a small site that requires no improvement may be able to fund the deal all on his own. "That's the dream! Own your business and the land it's on, outright!" she added.

Ross Blankenship, who owns two fenced contractor and fleet yards in Colorado's Vail Valley through Wins Parking, said the math has to work today. In a mountain market where little land is zoned for the use, he rents spaces for $210 a month for a car or pickup and $265 for a box truck or trailer, and charges $1,250 to $5,500 a month for contractor zones. Blankenship also runs Park Graph, the parking software he uses to rent the spaces.

The swing factor is vacancy, he said. "A full yard throws off more cash per dollar of capex than a small retail or office building. An empty one earns nothing," he said.

His advice for a first-time buyer: call 10 local contractors and ask what they pay for space.

"A small investor can still buy, but the deal has to work on rents you can collect today, not on what an institution might pay you later," Blankenship said.

#2811. They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'

Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience."

"Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam.

Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value.

As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal. On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware.

"People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target."

Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group.

In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says.

"The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved."

Delaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says.

Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says.

One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open."

From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds. Add a potential romantic connection to the mix, especially amid an ongoing "loneliness epidemic," and the urge to comply can be even harder to resist, she says.

If you feel yourself getting cornered in a situation where a recent acquaintance or romantic partner keeps asking for information you're not comfortable revealing, Delaney says it helps to have first practiced polite refusal. "One of my favorites is: They could just respond with: 'Why do you ask?'" she says. "Put the other person on the defensive. You could give a nondescript answer. You can say you don't know. You can say you can't respond."

If you're ever suspicious of a new connection — even if you don't want to be — do yourself a favor and conduct some basic vetting, she recommends. You might examine their social media profiles and other publicly available information, for example, to see if their story checks out.

If you can't find enough information to allay your suspicions, don't be shy about alerting your employer's security or human resources team, she says. For smaller companies, or scams outside the workplace, you can file a complaint for cyber threats or romance scams with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center.

And pay attention if your new paramour starts asking you specific questions about your finances or work credentials, says Delaney.

"If you have no game at home, and you get off an airplane somewhere and suddenly everyone's all over you, we call that a red flag," she says.

#2807. Hawks unable to outlast Bulls in overtime loss

The Atlanta Hawks were in action in the NBA Cup on Friday night but came up short in a 125-117 road loss in overtime against the Chicago Bulls. Jalen Johnson registered a triple-double of 27 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists and CJ McCollum added 20 points off the bench. For the Bulls — without star rookie Caleb Wilson — Norman Powell led the way with 33 points with seven Bulls scoring in double-digits.

The Hawks would have entered this game as favorites, with the Bulls heading into this game on the back of an eight-game losing streak and looking for just their second win of the season. Without impressive rookie Caleb Wilson, the Bulls were missing talent that is sorely needed and handed the Hawks a significant advantage with his absence. In reality, that is not how it played out.

The Hawks' time spent leading this game was extremely brief, and it was the Bulls who ran out to a double-digit lead in the first quarter behind 10 first quarter points from Powell. The key difference in this game began to become clear from the first quarter as the Hawks shot 2-of-8 from three-point range as the visitors' struggles shooting the ball became more concrete in the second quarter. The Bulls, meanwhile, had no problem dispatching their three-pointers and began to run their lead to a game-high 18 points in the second quarter.

While the Hawks found some success in the paint — and this was how they began to reign in the Chicago lead — the three-point shooting story was becoming clear: 3-of-17 for Atlanta, while the Bulls shot 11-of-28 from three in the first half. The Hawks were, at times, settling for transition, pull-up threes from above the break but only shot 1-of-11 from such shots in this game:

Off of a miss, Nickeil Alexander-Walker pushes the ball up the floor and springs into a three-pointer, but cannot convert:

Off of the pass from Dyson Daniels, Johnson pulls up into a three-pointer which is missed:

On this attempt, the Hawks work themselves into a better opportunity from above the break, with Alexander-Walker finding Daniels, who finds Onyeka Okongwu all alone above the break, but the three is missed:

The Hawks would continue to strike out on these opportunities all night long, and relied on the inside scoring of Johnson, and some tough, crafty baskets from McCollum to keep the visitors in range, even tying the game in late stages of the third quarter.

The Bulls, however, quickly stretched their lead back to 10 in the fourth quarter, giving the Hawks a lot of work to do on the road. Even with 2:22 remaining the Hawks faced an uphill battle of seven points, but Okongwu and Johnson, tied the game.

Having not led the game since the first quarter — when the game was 7-6 — the Hawks had multiple opportunities to take a late lead in this game. The first comes in the form of the Hawks failing to secure a rebound off of a missed shot from Jalen Smith, with Johnson losing the rebound and the Bulls get the opportunity to call a timeout:

After a missed shot from Powell inside, the Hawks get a chance to get out in transition. Johnson is faced by Josh Giddey, and elects to pass the ball back out to the perimeter to Alexander-Walker, who is unable to hit the three-pointer:

I'm not sure Johnson realized how strong his advantage was here: no help was coming, Giddey was on his own, and it's a one-on-one near the rim you would heavily back Johnson to score or draw a foul. Instead, he makes the unselfish play and finds Alexander-Walker, who continued his unfortunate shooting trend in this game at the wrong time.

The Hawks would get another chance as they advance the ball off of a timeout after another Bulls miss. Okongwu delivers a good pass to the cutting Aaron Wiggins, who is surely rim-side and through for a layup, but cannot complete the catch as the ball slips through his fingers and out of play:

Three differing chances for the Hawks to get/to score and all of them passed them by, and the game goes to overtime.

The Hawks would take their first lead since the first quarter, but it would not last, as Powell scored nine points in the overtime period to pull away from the Hawks before a dagger three Matas Buzelis dashes any hopes of a Hawks victory.

Postgame, Hawks head coach Quin Snyder highlighted the start of the game as an issue for the Hawks and discussed how the Hawks' shooting issues were exacerbated by the Bulls' own good three-point shooting night.

"We didn't play with the force at the beginning of the game," said Snyder postgame. "That impacts our defense, it's, kind of, the complimentary of basketball: how your defense affects your offense. When we're not forceful defensively, or active, and we're not running. We know the things we need to have in the front of our minds to focus on. When we don't do that, we don't play well. By the same token, we started to find that, 18 (points) down. When you're not shooting the ball well — we had a bad shooting night, which is going to happen — those things become even more important. When your opponent is shooting the ball, it compounds itself. We take from it what we can, and there's a lot here we can focus on."

"We've got to come out with energy from the jump, we just didn't do that," added Jalen Johnson.

This game can be summed up by living by the three and dying by the three. The Hawks finished with 8-of-40 from three (20%) while the Bulls shot 20-of-50 from three (40%), and while there are other nuances of this game that did not go the Hawks' way (which we'll touch on in a moment), the game can really be summed up as simply as that. If you hit eight threes while your opponent hits 20 (a 60-24 point disparity) it's difficult to win games consistently. The fact the Hawks almost did, speaks to the nature of the Bulls' season (allowing Jalen Smith to 15 shots and 1-of-6 from three is something the Bulls allowed to happen, for some reason).

From the Hawks' side, it was another difficult night shooting the three from Alexander-Walker, who shot 1-of-11 from three, and 6-of-19 from the field — it just wasn't his night, and there's been a couple of those this season where it becomes evident it may not be his night from three and he ends up with a poor percentage on a high volume. It was the same story across the board: reliable three-point shooters for the Hawks couldn't get their shots to fall. Okongwu shot 2-of-7 from three, while Aaron Wiggins shot 1-of-6 from distance.

Turnovers were also a key feature in this game, with the Hawks committing 17 in total, off of which the Bulls scored 20 points. These turnovers, as Snyder often references along with getting stops, impact the Hawks' ability to establish their identity: it's key for Atlanta to get out on the run in transition/off of a miss and when the Hawks are committing turnovers this impacts the Hawks significantly.

"It's hard to stop the ball when you turn the ball over," said CJ McCollum postgame.

Chicago turnovers were also how the Hawks remained in this game, scoring 34 points off of the Bulls' 24 turnovers — without these, the Hawks would not have been able to close the margin as they did, with Johnson and McCollum credited for 10 points apiece off of Chicago turnovers.

In addition, when the Hawks are off form from three, they are at least able to rack up points in the paint — many of which came off of turnovers — scoring 66 points in the paint, with Johnson accounting for 20 of these. Johnson finished with 27 points on 11-of-26 shooting from the field to go with his triple-double.

The Hawks were chasing the game for much of the affair, but Snyder didn't believe that this pursuit tired the Hawks physically.

"I didn't feel like we were tired," said Snyder. "Powell hit some tough shots in the overtime which I thought we defended pretty well. We made a couple of adjustments that our guys executed that I thought were really good. You put yourself in a position where you've got to make a lot of plays. We made enough to go to get where we were, but the game goes back and forth, and it went back one too many times."

There's no doubt the Hawks left themselves with a lot of work to do, both in the first half and in the fourth quarter when they trailed by double-digits. But they had their chances in regulation, and it slipped through their fingers (well, quite literally in Wiggins' case). In overtime, the quality of Powell (33 points on 12-of-29 shooting) shone through as he seized the game, with enough support from the rest to see the Bulls through.

It's a poor loss for the Hawks, who would have won this game had they hit any number of their 26 missed threes in regulation. They were also off since Monday, while the Bulls were in action on Wednesday, so their flat start to the game looks worse with context. In the context of the NBA Cup, the Hawks still have a positive point differential and are still in play to advance but cannot afford another loss such as this.

The Hawks (7-6) are back in action on Sunday when they will encounter another team on the road desperate for victory: the 1-12 Milwaukee Bucks.

#2806. Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic

Four researchers, a former journalist, a public policymaker, and an engineer founded Anthropic in 2021. Six years later, the artificial intelligence company is about to go public, with trading expected to begin on Nov. 19, in what will be one of the biggest IPOs on record.

Those seven co-founders are poised to each be worth many billions of dollars.

At the end of 2020, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei were vice presidents at OpenAI, the company that kicked off the generative AI frenzy with the launch of ChatGPT. But the two had grown frustrated with their employer over its approach to AI safety. Fearing a world where AI models' capabilities would progress faster than our understanding of them, the duo launched Anthropic early the next year.

They took a handful of OpenAI colleagues with them: Tom Brown, the company's research engineering lead on GPT-3; Jack Clark, a policy director; Jared Kaplan, a contract research consultant; and Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, both members of OpenAI's technical staff.

They were all deeply concerned about OpenAI's ambitions to focus on commercialization, and they now stand to be some of the first to cash in on the AI boom.

"They really started Anthropic not because they were hoping to get rich, but they started Anthropic because they like wanted to shape this really important thing in the world, and they thought that other people might do it worse than them," said Jeffrey Ladish, who joined Anthropic as a contract safety engineer in September 2021, and now serves as the executive director of AI safety institute Palisade Research.

Collectively the co-founders own about 10% of Anthropic. Each has about 240,000,000 class A shares, or about a 1.4% stake.

During Anthropic's most recent funding round, those shares — valued at $58.90 each — amounted to about $14 billion in value for each co-founder. If Anthropic's IPO reaches its target of $70 to $78 per share, or a market valuation of nearly $1.4 trillion, it would push those stakes to $17 billion to $18 billion.

"It's extremely hard not to be influenced by your incentives," Ladish said. "You have investors, and money is not just like an end; it's also a means."

Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.

The face of Anthropic is CEO Dario Amodei. He holds the most shares of the bunch: 245,259,100 including shares subject to voting proxies.

Amodei, 43, didn't get his start in business. He comes from the world of research, obtaining a doctorate in computational neuroscience from Princeton University in 2011. He then went to work at Stanford University as a postdoctoral scholar from 2011 to 2014.

Even in the private sector, Amodei's experience was focused on research. He worked at China's Baidu, leading research on speech recognition from 2014 to 2015, followed by a stint at Google Brain working on deep learning and neural networks, foundational scientific frameworks for today's large language models. He joined OpenAI in July 2016.

On the Big Technology podcast in July 2025, Amodei said he got into AI to solve the "almost intractable" and "slow moving" problems of biology.

"I think my reason to start a company was that I had worked at other companies and I just didn't feel like the way those companies were run was really oriented towards trying to have that impact," he said, adding that the desire for impact was often used by companies as an insincere ploy to recruit talent.

At OpenAI, Amodei is credited with co-inventing reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), alongside Anthropic co-founder, Tom Brown. RLHF is a fine-tuning method used to align model outputs with human needs. That could mean training a model to speak politely or to not offer violent or harmful solutions to problems.

Four years her brother's junior, Daniela Amodei, 39, serves as the president and board chair of Anthropic. The Amodeis are both San Francisco natives, growing up in the Mission District, just a few miles away from Anthropic's current headquarters.

The pair were teenagers during the height of the dot-com bubble and its subsequent fallout, both attending Lowell High School, a magnet school and one of the most prestigious public schools in the country. After graduating, Daniela went on to study English literature and politics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, earning her degree in 2009.

Daniela started her career in politics, working for Matt Cartwright, a Democrat representing what was then Pennsylvania's 17th congressional district, and then moved into tech, taking on various roles in risk management at Stripe for five years.

In a June interview with Stanford's Graduate School of Business, she said her experience in politics, specifically campaigns, naturally led her to startups and Silicon Valley.

"I was like, 'Wow, a small number of people that work really hard, who are young and driven, can really change the world,'" she said.

Anthropic's chief compute officer, Tom Brown, 39, is perhaps the most entrepreneurial of the bunch. After graduating from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a Master of Engineering in 2010, Brown went on to found two startups, MoPub and Grouper.

MoPub was a mobile advertising business acquired by Twitter in 2013. There he served as founding engineer in 2011. Grouper, where Brown served as co-founder and technology chief, was a Y Combinator-backed group dating app.

After Grouper, Brown pivoted to research, sharing on Y Combinator's Lightcone podcast in August 2025 that he was self-taught on machine learning research, a daunting task since he received a B- in linear algebra at university.

"I kind of flip-flopped on it for six months trying to build up courage to" make the switch, he said.

Alongside co-inventing RLHF, as a researcher at OpenAI, Brown led the training efforts on GPT-3, a model that marked a historic leap from GPT-2, going from 1.5 billion parameters to 175 billion.

Jack Clark, 37, the head of public benefit at Anthropic, left his career as a journalist in 2016 to work at OpenAI. Clark is now also the leader of the Anthropic Institute, the company's internal think tank that explores AI's social and economic impacts.

A native of the U.K., Clark grew up in the seaside town of Brighton and later studied English literature and creative writing at the University of East Anglia. He then went on to write for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

In an email to a colleague at Bloomberg at the time, Clark said his decision to leave journalism was because he had "never believed in something strongly before" and that he needed to join OpenAI "and live with the consequences, which I hope are good."

Kaplan, 42, Anthropic's chief science officer, still holds a position as an associate professor in the department of physics and astronomy at Johns Hopkins University. The theoretical physicist got his PhD in physics from Harvard in 2009, working for four years after as a postdoctoral fellow at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, a particle physics research facility run by Stanford and funded by the Department of Energy.

Kaplan co-pioneered scaling laws, or the notion that large language models get exponentially better when trained on larger and larger data sets, alongside Dario Amodei. He also pioneered "constitutional AI," or a method of aligning models by using a list of safety principles and policies. His day-to-day work concerns safety assessments for models, responsible scaling policy at the company, and existential risks.

In an interview with The Guardian in December 2025, Kaplan noted that the decision over whether or not to let AI "recursively self improve," or write the code to enhance itself without a human in the loop, would be "in some ways the ultimate risk, because it's kind of like letting AI kind of go," and that he expects this risk will be taken sometime between 2027 and 2030.

Anthropic's chief architect, Sam McCandlish, 36, came to OpenAI as a fellow focused on AI safety. He also led early research on coding tool Codex, which now constitutes a significant portion of OpenAI's revenue.

McCandlish claims he and the rest of the Anthropic co-founders were not following an entrepreneurial spirit when they charted out on their own. In a December 2024 video from Anthropic's YouTube channel, he said, "None of us wanted to found a company. We just felt like it was our duty."

McCandlish, like Kaplan, also came from the world of academia, completing his PhD in theoretical and mathematical physics at Stanford in 2017 and working at Boston University as a postdoctoral fellow the year afterward. His work focused on quantum gravity and tensor networks.

Now, his work focuses on pre-training, or the first step of training a large language model on swaths of data, among other things.

Chris Olah, 34, heads Anthropic's interpretability research, a branch of study in machine learning that attempts to understand how a large language model "thinks" — or rather, which data inputs and reasoning methods it uses to arrive at its outputs.

Like McCandlish, Olah was not originally keen on starting a company. In the same December 2024 YouTube video, Olah said, "I was arguing for a long time that we should do a nonprofit instead, and just focus on safety research."

Olah had a nontraditional path to Anthropic, dropping out of the University of Toronto after one year and working for short stints as a developer at the government agency Environment Canada and software startup Xelerance.

His career truly took off when he was awarded a Thiel Fellowship in 2012, which he used to pursue research pertaining to 3D printers for two years. He then joined Google Brain, first as an intern and then as a researcher, before moving to OpenAI in 2018.

While together the seven founders may only own about 10% of total equity, they will have a majority vote. Founder LLC, the legal entity set up that owns a single Class F share, gives Anthropic's co-founders a 50.1% majority voting control over the company. While Benjamin Mann, a member of Anthropic's technical staff and also an ex-OpenAI employee, is often called a co-founder, he is not an owner of Founder LLC.

The co-founders are expected to collectively sell over 20 million shares during the IPO, resulting in roughly $250 million in cash per founder, according to Anthropic's prospectus.

They plan to dedicate 80% of the wealth from their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropy, according to the IPO filing, though the pledge isn't legally binding. Anthropic is also setting aside 5% of its shares to form a new public benefit fund — to finance nonprofits, research, and potentially direct community grants — with potential to grow the size of the fund as the company itself grows.

#2805. Ex-NFL punter sues NCAA after heartbreaking Parkinson’s diagnosis

A former NFL star turned orthopedic surgeon is suing the NCAA, claiming his medical career is finished after repeated concussions he suffered as a college athlete led him to develop Parkinson's disease.

Patrick O'Neill, 55, was an Academic All-American and University Scholar at Syracuse University, where he played on a football scholarship from 1990-1993.

He claims that during his collegiate football days, he was urged to power through head injuries and was kept in the dark about their risks.

New England Patriots punter Patrick O'Neill was named the NFL All-rookie punter during his first pro season. Getty Images

"The NCAA failed to protect Patrick O'Neill's health and safety, because it failed to make the game of football as safe as possible, and because it failed to keep Patrick O'Neill informed so he could make reasonable decisions about whether to play college football and how to play it safely," says the suit against the NCAA, filed Nov. 2 in Manhattan Supreme Court.

After graduating, O'Neill was drafted in 1994 as an NFL punter and played for the New England Patriots, Chicago Bears, New York Jets and Jacksonville Jaguars. He was named the NFL All-rookie punter during his first pro season with the Patriots.

But he soon left the NFL to pursue his real dream — becoming a doctor. In 1998 he was accepted into John Hopkins University Medical School in Baltimore.

The MD launched a successful career as a surgeon and became the chief of orthopedic surgery at Sarasota Memorial Hospital.

O'Neill said his ability to practice medicine has been affected. sarasotafootandankle.com

He currently practices at Kennedy-White Orthopedic Center in Sarasota, Florida. He's the only board-certified fellowship-trained foot and ankle orthopedic surgeon in the county.

"This brain disease has forced Patrick O'Neill to suffer great loss, including in his ability to practice as an orthopedic surgeon," the complaint claims.

The degenerative disease can cause tremors, slowed movement and other symptoms that grow progressively worse.

O'Neill seen in his college football days. Syracuse

O'Neill contends in court docs the NCAA knew about the dangers of repeated head trauma but failed to warn or protect its athletes.

O'Neill blames the NCAA for its lack of concussion-related regulations, alleging the organization knew repeated head injuries were linked to Parkinson's disease as far back as the 1930s, but failed to take adequate steps to protect players.

The lawsuit alleges that the NCAA ignored doctor recommendations to ban players from contact sports after suffering three moderate concussions.

"Without a competent medical professionals properly versed in repetitive head trauma on the sidelines, Patrick O'Neill repeatedly sustained trauma to his head in games and/or practice in NCAA football," the complaint alleges.

"Despite the trauma, Patrick O'Neill was never removed from the field for examination, rest, and treatment."

The NCAA, Syracuse University, O'Neill and his attorney did not return requests for comment.

#2804. Draymond Green defends Rockets from ‘dirty' label after Steph Curry injury

Draymond Green defends Rockets from 'dirty' label after Steph Curry injury originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Draymond Green does not think the Houston Rockets are a dirty team. He does, however, believe they are a very physical one.

Speaking on "The Draymond Green Show" as he discussed Steph Curry's injury and playing without him, Green addressed the label that followed the Warriors' 115-108 loss in Houston on Nov. 11. Curry grimaced and reached for his right side after tangling with Rockets center Alperen Sengun on a screen early in the first quarter, leaving the game minutes later.

An MRI confirmed an oblique abdominal tear, and Curry will be re-evaluated in two weeks, with ESPN's Shams Charania reporting the team expects him to miss closer to a month. Some fans blamed Sengun, yet Green explains the team is just outright physical, not dirty.

"I know a lot of people are saying, 'Oh man, the Houston Rockets are a dirty team.' I don't get off into that dirty thing," Green said. "Every now and then you see some people that just do things that are downright dirty, and it happens, and when it does, I'll speak on it."

The matchup has been physical before. Curry left a Warriors loss to Houston last November with a right quad contusion after a collision with Amen Thompson and a screen by Sengun.

Wednesday's game saw Rockets guard Marcus Smart ejected for throwing a punch that grazed the nose of Warriors center Charles Bassey, and the NBA suspended Smart three games. Bassey said Smart was playing dirty "the whole game" and called the punch "fake toughness."

Green drew a different line. He said the thing that bothers him most about Houston is not rough play.

"Do they do some bulls— when we play them? Absolutely," Green said. "I think the thing that may irritate me the most is, like, they play super physical, but then they start flopping sometimes, you know. And so I would say that irritates me more, but I'm not going to sit here and call them a dirty team. They're a physical team."

"When we were watching film pregame, you can see on the film they are physical as hell, and so give them credit," Green said.

Green will speak up when something truly is dirty. In his eyes, the Rockets are just physical

#2803. $180 million Van Gogh tests the art market and collector confidence

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox.

The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades.

Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million.

The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century.

Sotheby's CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors.

"There's been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets," Stewart said. "It's a global phenomenon. We're seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S."

Christie's star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky's "Betonte Ecken," estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie's CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is "confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works." She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren't likely to deter serious collectors.

"At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view," Brennan said. "They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling."

The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America.

Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half.

"Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic," Watson said. "Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales."

INDIANAPOLIS — Josh Hart's issues aren't exclusive to his shot. The Knicks veteran said he's mentally struggling to start a disappointing season, and he doesn't know how to break out of it.

"Wish I could tell you," Hart said. "Don't know. Right now I'm not in a good head space and I got to figure out how to improve that. And improve my play."

Asked what that meant, Hart, who is shooting just 36 percent on the season, said, "Just mentally. Got to be better mentally. Got to figure stuff out."

Josh Hart of the New York Knicks shoots a 3-pointer against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Hart finished scoreless Friday night and was benched for the entire fourth quarter of a 106-104 loss to the Pacers, among the low points of a season that has never been on track for the 31-year-old.

He's up for an extension, but the Knicks put out a statement in October declaring they're shutting down all negotiations, including Hart's and Karl-Anthony Towns'.

Hart revealed Friday that he suffered a calf injury before training camp, which set back his conditioning. He then hurt his ankle and missed three games.

The Knicks are stacked with wings and guards, creating congestion and sporadic playing time. Mikal Bridges has also been benched, as coach Mike Brown leaned on Landry Shamet and Miles McBride.

Brown acknowledged that finding time for Bridges and Hart could be difficult.

Josh Hart, left, speaks with New York Knicks teammate Mikal Bridges during a game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"There are several different ways you can look at it," Hart said. "You can look at it, if they have it going, cool. Good. You could look at it like, 'OK, maybe something else has to change.'"

Hart didn't specify the "change," but logic indicates he meant a trade. Three years ago, Leon Rose faced a similar conundrum. Too many guards, not enough minutes.

So Rose traded two — RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley — for a bigger forward in OG Anunoby.

Beginning Sunday, the Knicks face Barrett and Quickley twice in three days in Toronto, while Hart tries to find a better headspace.

#2798. Purdue 7 Iowa 28: Game Wrap

Purdue's travel to Iowa City was interrupted after its flight was delayed by a nationwide grounding of planes on Friday evening, though it ultimately mattered very little on Saturday as the Boilermakers were grounded by the Hawkeyes as well. The Boilermakers never looked like a legitimate threat to the Hawkeyes, who controlled nearly every aspect of the game and prevented Purdue from seizing the momentum needed to pull off an upset. Much like the weeks following Purdue's bye, the contest unfolded with Iowa generating explosive plays and dominating both sides of the line of scrimmage.

As it has for much of the season, Purdue's offense moved the ball effectively on its opening possession, driving deep into Iowa territory. However, any early momentum—and any hope of forcing the Hawkeyes to play from behind—evaporated when typically reliable freshman kicker Jacobo Echeverria Lozano missed a 38-yard field goal attempt. From that point forward, the game proceeded much as expected.

The Boilermakers' defense struggled immediately on its first series, getting flagged four times and failing to make the stops necessary to slow down a Hawkeye offense that has been steady, if unspectacular, all season. That opening possession foreshadowed how Iowa would operate all afternoon, as the Hawkeyes marched 80 yards in nearly seven minutes before capping the drive with a 1-yard touchdown plunge from quarterback Hank Brown.

Head coach Barry Odom announced the firing of defensive coordinator Kevin Kane following the loss to Maryland, yet Purdue's defense looked much the same as it has all year. Rather than taking over play-calling duties himself, Odom tabbed defensive analyst Dave Steckel to run the unit. A former defensive coordinator whom Odom has worked with previously, Steckel did not implement any drastic schematic changes, and the surrendering of explosive plays and inability to get off the field on third down continued. Iowa recorded eight big plays, including seven on the ground that accounted for 138 yards.

The first half was largely lopsided, though the Boilermakers battled back to cut the deficit to 14-7 with under two minutes remaining in the second quarter on a Ryan Browne touchdown pass to George Burhenn—his third touchdown of the season. That proved to be Purdue's lone trip to the end zone. Whatever momentum the offense had built quickly vanished when the defense surrendered a touchdown with less than 10 seconds left before halftime on a play eerily reminiscent of Maryland's 87-yard score. That 21-7 deficit effectively sealed Purdue's fate before the second half even began.

Whatever slim margin for error Purdue still possessed disappeared immediately after the break, as Iowa opened the third quarter with a 75-yard touchdown drive to push its lead to 28-7. The Hawkeyes continued to dictate the pace offensively, racking up 246 rushing yards and converting 10 of 15 third-down attempts. Purdue needed to force Iowa to rely on Hank Brown's arm, but instead, the Hawkeyes imposed their will by controlling the line of scrimmage.

That 28-7 margin held as the final score, as the Boilermakers were unable to reach the end zone again. Browne did manage to move the offense into scoring position, but an ill-advised throw into the end zone resulted in an interception. That marked the lone turnover for Browne, who finished 14-of-23 passing for 158 yards and one touchdown. Purdue failed to eclipse 100 net rushing yards for the third time in four games, a deficiency that has placed mounting pressure on Browne to carry the offense. Ijeboi paced the Boilermakers with 64 yards on 15 carries, though the unit as a whole continued to struggle at converting scoring opportunities, leaving at least 10 points on the field.

By the final whistle, Purdue had been outgained 434-304, a stark contrast to the promise the team showed during the first six weeks of the campaign. Standing at 3-3 with victories over Minnesota and Illinois—alongside a double-overtime loss to a Wake Forest squad potentially headed for the Top 10—the Boilermakers entered their bye week with postseason aspirations squarely in sight. Instead, Purdue fell to 3-7 with games remaining against Wisconsin and Indiana, making a 3-9 finish look increasingly likely.

That trajectory offers little solace to a fan base that was dealt a difficult hand with the hiring of Kevin Kane and has been forced to watch an offense devoid of the innovative looks seen across most of modern college football.

#2797. Heating oil prices are up 59% from last winter. The spike is 'crushing folks,' Maine nonprofit says

Winter heating bills can strain household budgets. This year, a spike in heating oil prices could make the season especially difficult for households that depend on the fuel and have little financial wiggle room.

The national average price of heating oil was roughly $5.91 a gallon as of Nov. 9, up about $2.19, or 59%, from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In Maine, the average price per gallon is roughly $5.83, up about $2.49 from a year earlier, or about 75%. The state is among those whose residents may feel the price rise acutely — about 50% of homes there use heating oil.

The jump "is crushing folks," said Jason Parent, CEO of AVEC Community Action, a nonprofit agency based in Presque Isle, Maine, that provides heating assistance and other social services in three of the state's 16 counties. Many residents face immediate crises, he said, such as empty fuel tanks or reliance on unsafe heating sources.

"My fear is that there are households out there who have secondary fuel sources like wood stoves, pellet stoves and other things that are no longer operating and functioning in a safe way," Parent said.

The price surge comes on the heels of years of high overall inflation that has already squeezed household budgets, he said.

"The cost of living has made it impossible for households who had been figuring out how to get by without [financial help]," Parent said.

The price spike comes amid a tight global market for refined fuels, a category that includes heating oil and diesel. Supply shocks tied to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war, low inventories and limited refining capacity have constrained supplies and added upward pressure on fuel prices, according to recent research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.

The EIA predicts that a warmer winter in the Northeast will reduce consumption, helping to offset higher prices. In October, the agency forecast that the average household using heating oil will spend $2,115 from November through March, about 21% more than last year.

Meanwhile, homes primarily heated with natural gas are expected to spend an average of $640 this winter, down 9%, while those using propane are forecast to spend an average of $1,246, down 3%, according to the EIA's October forecast. Households using electricity for heating are expected to spend an average of $1,196, up 4% from a year ago. These are national figures.

Roughly 4.1 million U.S. households use heating oil as their primary means of heating their homes, according to the EIA. Most of them — close to 3.4 million — are located in the Northeast.

Unlike electricity or natural gas, heating oil is delivered in large quantities. Payment terms vary, but some dealers require a minimum delivery or charge extra for smaller orders. In Maine, for example, ordering at least 100 gallons for a standard 275-gallon tank can avoid a surcharge, according to the state attorney general's office. At current prices, that 100 gallons would cost about $600 — a tall order for some households.

AVEC's Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, provides financial assistance to qualifying households, based primarily on income and the number of people living in the home. Funding originates with the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, which is run by the U.S. Health and Human Services Department and overseen by state agencies, often working with local organizations such as AVEC.

Maine and tribal grantees in the state received about $38 million from LIHEAP in October, according to a press release from outgoing Republican Sen. Susan Collins. AVEC administers about $4 million of that through HEAP, Parent said. AVEC also gets donations from community fundraising to help residents cover heating costs.

A component of HEAP is the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which serves qualifying families who face an energy crisis, such as a potential electric shutoff or an empty oil tank and no financial means to replenish the supply.

AVEC began taking calls for that program on Nov. 2, Parent said.

"In the first hour alone, there were 150 voicemail messages on our emergency fuel line," Parent said. "People were in crisis before the program opened up."

Catherine Lafleche of Hersey, Maine, describes AVEC as a lifeline.

The 65-year-old is guardian to two grandchildren, ages 11 and 6, and is living mostly on about $1,100 in monthly Social Security benefits and state guardianship assistance, after shattering her upper-arm bone in a fall in April. Her injury required reverse shoulder replacement surgery, from which she continues to recover. Before that fall, she had worked as a substitute teacher and bookkeeper.

"I'm $6,000 short of income at this point in the year," Lafleche said.

Hersey is in Maine's northernmost county, Aroostook, where January and February bring average high temperatures in the 20s and average lows in the single digits, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data from 1991 to 2020 recorded at a Caribou Municipal Airport weather station. Last winter, the area experienced severe cold snaps, including on Jan. 24, when the high was minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit.

Lafleche applied to HEAP through AVEC in August, but a backlog meant potentially waiting until November for assistance. Unable to afford more fuel when it became chilly, she ran out of heating oil in early October and relied on a small wood stove to keep part of her house warm, burning Amazon boxes collected from other local residents because she didn't have enough firewood.

In late October, an AVEC representative called to say a charitable donation would cover 100 gallons of heating oil.

"When the oil man came, I cried," Lafleche said.

For residents in Maine who need help covering the cost to heat their homes and are seeking out help, "the need is outpacing the benefits," said Parent, of AVEC.

The average benefit through HEAP is about $750 per household this season, up from roughly $550 a year ago, Parent said. "That $750 is going less far than the $550 did last season" for heating oil, he said. "It's buying fewer gallons because of the precipitous increase."

The benefits are generally paid directly to the fuel supplier as a credit on the household's account. Even if a household qualifies, funding may run out.

"We're in a world of hurt now ... but it's going to be crisis time again in January or February," Parent said.

The Trump administration, in an effort to bring down heating oil prices, said it would release 300,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, according to a Nov. 4 release from the U.S. Energy Department.

Whether adding this extra heating oil to the market will reduce prices for residents depends at least partly on how it gets doled out, said Jonathan Rubin, director of the Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center and a professor of economics at the University of Maine.

"No one really knows the economic impact, because will the home-heating oil distributors release it in one month, which would make it about 10% to 12% of a single month's supply? Or will they release it over the entire season, in which case it's only about one and a half percent of the entire season's home heating oil supply?" Rubin said.

"I would say that this is a modest short-term buffer," he said.

Congressional lawmakers have called for increased LIHEAP funding this year due to rising energy costs, including heating oil. Dozens of House lawmakers — mostly Democrats — signed an Oct. 14 letter to the House Appropriations Committee seeking an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental funding for LIHEAP.

That followed an Oct. 1 letter from a group of Democratic senators and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Health and Human Services, also asking that he seek at least $3 billion more for LIHEAP.

Already, the government released roughly $3.63 billion in LIHEAP funding nationwide on Oct. 9 — 90% of the roughly $4 billion available under a continuing resolution that is currently funding federal agencies.

The timing for disbursing the remainder depends on when Congress either passes full-year funding for the 2027 fiscal year — which started Oct. 1 and runs through Sept. 30, 2027 — or passes another stopgap measure to keep the government running. If lawmakers do neither by Dec. 11, a federal shutdown would begin.

Whether the additional $3 billion requested for LIHEAP will be considered in any upcoming congressional appropriations process is uncertain.

Lafleche, the Hersey resident, said the 100 gallons of heating oil donated to her, along with some firewood she has now purchased, should keep her home warm until early December. She hopes to receive approval for benefits by then through HEAP, which has helped her in past years.

"We're not in this position by choice. Most of us made every plan to the contrary, but it stacked up to be not enough. And I feel like we don't deserve to be cold," she said.

#2796. The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly: Duke Blue Devils 2026 Edition

It was maybe a bit more fraught than we'd have liked, but Miami got back to their winning ways on Saturday afternoon with a 36-25 homecoming win over the Duke Blue Devils.

Craig T. Smith has your game recap, and Mike Schiffman has your 3 stars. Links below!

And now, let's dive into The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly

A win! Winning isn't easy, and I will never take it for granted, regardless of opponent.

QB Darian Mensah. The #HeisMensah campaign continues. 30/41 passing (73.2% completions) for 382 yards with 1 touchdown and 0 interceptions, 4 carries, 7 yards rushing.

Mensah's cumulative stats: 241/317 passing, 76.0% completions, 3,083 yards, 29 touchdowns, 2 interception, 39 carries, 144 yards, 2 touchdowns.

RB Javian Mallory. Mark Fletcher Jr. didn't play after halftime, and the superstar stepped up huge. 10 carries for 71 yards and 2 touchdowns, and 3 catches for 79 yards and a touchdown. Just a monster performance, with nearly all his yards and all 3 touchdowns coming in the 2nd half.

WR Cooper Barkate. 8 catches for 134 yards. Looked like the Barkate we saw at Duke last year…just AGAINST Duke this year.

RB Jordan Lyle. 7 carries for 54 yards. And, more importantly, he's starting to look like HIMSELF again, not this shell of a player we've seen for the last 25 games across 2 years. That's big for Miami moving forward.

WRs Daylyn Upshaw and Vandrevius Jacobs, and TE Elija Lofton all had 5+ catches as well, and solid (if imperfect) play.

S Dylan Dyan and JJ Dunnigan both had 6 tackles, and Dunnigan had a TFL. Again, solid if imperfect.

S Bryce Fitzgerald had 3 tackles, a TFL, and a PBU (but the latter should have been a pick-6. I still can't believe he dropped that).

EDGE Third Scroggins with one of the only pressures of the day. Great rush by him. Needs more snaps.

K Jake Weinberg. 3/3 on FGs, perfect on PATs, and good kickoffs. The one kickoff that was returned was because the kick came from our 20 after a penalty to end the previous drive. Not his fault.

He did everything he could, and it was a tour de force performance. He's a Heisman finalist in my eyes. Incredible player. Bravo.

Nice coverage and PBU by Xavier Lucas on to end Duke's first drive. That's what I'm talking about, defense!

DBs Damari Brown, Xavier Lucas, and Ethan O'Connor playing through the whistle to get late PBUs on Duke's first few drives.

S J.J. Dunnigan with a solid tackle (for a loss even!) on a shallow crosser to end Duke's second possession.

EDGE Herbert "Third" Scroggins III with a nice rush move to get pressure on the play that ended with the Dunnigan TFL. Good to see someone start winning up front along the DL.
