#2770. Kenny Dillingham had last-minute idea for Mikey Keene in ASU football win at UCF

ORLANDO — Mikey Keene's homecoming moment wasn't planned.

"I'm bad at preparing for stuff like that," Arizona State head coach Kenny Dillingham said.

But with the Sun Devils ahead 26-13 in the final two minutes during their road trip to UCF on Nov. 14, Dillingham had an epiphany and subbed Keene in at quarterback.

The sixth-year senior began his college career with two years at UCF. With freshman Jake Fette starting for ASU these days and Keene in his final season of eligibility, this trip to Acrisure Bounce House might've marked the end of his career, too.

Keene took two kneel-downs to drain the last minute from the clock and secure bowl eligibility.

"It was more like last-minute, I noticed it," Dillingham said. "I was like, 'Oh, yeah, Mikey. We've got to get him in to kneel it down. There's a special moment for him.'"

UCF recruited Keene as a three-star prospect out of Chandler, Arizona. As a freshman in 2021, he immediately became the backup to Dillon Gabriel — and then rose to starter after Gabriel broke his clavicle three games in.

Keene played 11 contests and showed plenty of promise. He completed 64% of his passes for 1,730 yards, 17 touchdowns and six interceptions.

He also gave Gus Malzahn his signature triumph as UCF's head coach. Keene is the last QB to lead the Knights to a bowl win, upsetting Florida in the 2021 Gasparilla Bowl.

He returned and served as John Rhys Plumlee's backup in 2022 before hitting the transfer portal. He's been a frequent flyer there, transferring to Fresno State, Michigan and Arizona State since bolting from Orlando.

Keene has made one start in his first fall with ASU.

If he does not see the field the rest of the year, he'll have a good story to tell about the final, impromptu snaps of his career.

The Eagles drafted eight players in April and seven of them have seen game action over the first half of the season, but to varying degrees.

With the Eagles on their Week 10 bye week, let's recap the first half of the season for all eight of their draft picks:

After some disappointing moments early in his rookie season, we have seen a ton of growth from Makai Lemon recently. Without DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks for three weeks, Lemon has had the three best games of his rookie season against the Cowboys (7 catches for 67 yards, 1 TD), Commanders (6 catches for 57 yards) and Giants (6 catches for 61 yards). While Lemon was tough on himself for a couple drops in Week 9, he has been one of the few bright spots recently.

Through nine games, Lemon has been targeted 54 times and has 37 catches for 312 yards and a touchdown. He's on pace for 102 targets, 70 catches, 589 yards and 2 touchdowns. But it's also worth noting that his numbers have been improving as the season goes on.

Here's a look at the Eagles' rookie records for receptions and receiving yards. Lemon is on pace to finish his season second on the receptions list and ninth in receiving yards. But hopefully the Eagles have scrapped all those behind-the-line passes to him.

Through nine weeks, Lemon is tied with KC Conception for the lead among rookies in receptions and is fourth in receiving yards among rookies behind Denzel Boston (507), Concepcion (437) and Carnell Tate (413).

After a rough training camp, Eli Stowers dealt with a quad injury that kept him on IR for the first six weeks of the season. He made his NFL debut a few weeks ago against the Cowboys, but hasn't played a ton on offense yet. Here's a look at his offensive snap counts for these last three weeks.

Week 7 vs. DAL: 12 snapsWeek 8 at WAS: 13 snapsWeek 9 vs. NYG: 7 snaps

Overall, Stowers has been targeted 5 times and has 3 catches for 53 yards. All three of those catches came in the loss to Washington and two of them came very late in the fourth quarter. His long of 34 yards came at the very end of the game.

But Stowers hasn't looked out of place in limited action. He has been doing some good things away from the football and has shown a real willingness to do some dirty work and block. While blocking is probably never going to be his strength, he needed to improve in that area and is clearly working on it. But in this lost season, it would make sense to see more of Stowers in the second half.

In addition to his work on offense, Stowers has also played 27 special teams snaps. That's something new for him because he began his college career as a quarterback and then became a star tight end. But he's working hard at that too.

The plan was for Markel Bell to sit all season and learn behind Jordan Mailata and Lane Johnson. But that plan got tossed in the garbage can early this season when Johnson abruptly retired. Bell was thrust into the starting lineup in Week 4 against the Rams and has started the last six games with plenty of ups and downs.

Early in his time as a starter, Bell looked really promising and looked to be settling into that role. But the last couple of games have been much rougher for the 6-foot-9 rookie. In six starts this season, according to ProFootballFocus, Bell has given up 5 sacks and 19 pressures, but 3 of those sacks came in his late-notice start against the Rams in Week 4.

There's a really good chance that veteran Fred Johnson would be a better option right now, but the Eagles should ride this out with Bell to figure out if he really has the potential to be a long-term replacement for Johnson. We'll probably learn a lot about him over the second half of this season.

Round 5-178: Cole Payton, QB, North Dakota State

The Eagles made sure to give Cole Payton plenty of reps in training camp despite having three quarterbacks on the depth chart ahead of him. But Payton has been inactive five times this season and has been active but hasn't played three times. Back in Week 5 against the Jaguars, Payton played 10 snaps on special teams and that's the only time he has seen the field.

The idea of Payton on special teams is fun, especially in a lost season like this. Maybe the Eagles will get him some more reps in that role or perhaps find a way to get him on the field on offense. Joe Milton and Tanner McKee are both still ahead of Payton on the depth chart but the way this season is going, would you be surprised to see Payton eventually get on the field as a starter?

When the Eagles drafted Micah Morris in the sixth round, he was expected to be a developmental pick and that has held true. Through 9 games, Morris has played one snap on offense and 19 on special teams. Morris has been active the last seven weeks but hasn't needed to play. If this season continues to spiral, maybe we'll get to see what Morris can do.

Round 7-244: Cole Wisniewski, S, Texas Tech

Because Cole Wisniewski missed most of training camp with injuries (hamstring and concussion), he never really had much of a shot to make the Eagles' 53-man roster. But once Wisniewski cleared waivers, the Eagles signed him to the practice squad and he has been there all season. Through nine games, Wisniewski has been elevated twice and has played 36 snaps on special teams. He has one elevation remaining.

The Eagles knew Uar Bernard was a long-term project when they drafted him and that is playing out. Bernard has next-level athleticism but is extremely raw so he needs to continue to learn the game. After the Eagles waived him at final cuts, they signed him to the practice squad. Unfortunately, Bernard suffered an injury in practice and has been on the Practice Squad Injured list back on Oct. 9. So this project is on hold for now.

Round 7-252: Keyshawn James-Newby, Edge, New Mexico

There was a lot of hand-wringing from fans in the summer when the Eagles attempted to get both Bernard and Josh Weru through waivers to the practice squad. The Eagles were probably more concerned about Keyshawn James-Newby. Because even though the seventh-round pick missed most of training camp with an ankle injury, he did flash in his preseason action. But James-Newby cleared waivers and has been on the practice squad all season.

The Eagles have used up two of his three elevations this season. James-Newby played 48 defensive snaps in his NFL debut against the Panthers and then 4 the following week against the Panthers. He has a couple of combined tackles in his defensive action. He has also played 40 special teams snaps.

The Eagles signed the 24-year-old long snapper after the draft and he has played in every game this season — totaling 77 special teams snaps. He has 3 combined tackles and a fumble recovery. He was able to show some hustle when he jumped on a muffed punt against the Giants. Underwood appears to be working well with punter Braden Mann and kicker Jake Elliott.

#2768. Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

SACRAMENTO ― The Sacramento Kings have dropped another game and if you think head coach Doug Christie is worried about being in some kind of hot seat, he's not. And he shouldn't be.

It's a familiar position for Christie, who's been dealt a bad hand since his head coaching tenure began. He inherited a then-Mike Brown team that was a season removed from the postseason before eventually trading its franchise player, De'Aaron Fox. They finished 40-42, Christie went 27-24 as interim, having taken over after a 13-18 start.

Last season, as an official first-year coach, without the interim tag, multiple players in his projected lineup, including Domantas Sabonis and Keegan Murray, missed large portions of the season, and the Kings finished with its worst record in franchise history since moving to Sacramento at 22-60.

And now, the Kings are having one of the worst starts in franchise history, dropping to 1-11 after their Friday night loss to the Portland Trail Blazers, 120-107, on Nov. 13 during the NBA Cup. It's the worst start since the 1990-91 season, in which that team started 1-13.

"I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY about potentially being in the hot seat. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number."

When Scott Perry became Kings general manager in April 2025, one of his first moves was to sign Christie to a three-year deal, worth about $2 million per year with a team option in the final year, 2027-28. Christie remained leading the charge after coaching to the worst franchise record in team history since 2008-2009 (17-65), as Perry attributed that tumultuous season to injuries, according to The Athletic.

It's much of the same this season, with a season-ending injury to Ben Simmons and second-year center Maxime Raynaud missing the start of the season with a knee injury.

"We come in, continue to teach, continue to push," Christie said. "As we get all these guys back and get them healthy, and then we continue down the path of trying to put together what we thought we would be putting together when we started this process."

The Kings are reportedly hesitant to part ways with Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick. Former Sacramento Kings legend and current Sacramento State head coach Mike Bibby sat front row to get a witness of the the beatdown handed to the Kings.

The former guard, who played in Sacramento from 2001-2008, showed support for his former teammate, saying he wasn't the one to blame during a postgame appearance with Morgan Ragan and Deuce Mason on NBC Sports California.

"I don't blame Doug (Christie)," Bibby said. "I don't think Doug is the problem. Doug's been there for a long time, I think Doug could help, but getting rid of Doug's not the problem."

However, Bibby did say it was "time for some changes". Although he wasn't sure where those changes needed to come from, he advised the team to trade guys like Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Malik Monk to put them in better positions while the Kings start over. It happened to Bibby in his day when the Kings were no longer winning and they traded him to the Atlanta Hawks in 2008.

"When I was here I didn't wanna leave, but it was time to go," Bibby said. "For those guys put them in good situations like Sabonis, LaVine, put them in situations that could help them and get some good stuff back. It's going to take a couple of years to get the Kings going again."

Kings: Darius Acuff Jr. is making history, but is losing taking a toll?

If there's one thing Christie knows, it's how hard the Sacramento fans go for the Kings. He's experienced it as a player, and as both assistant and head coach he's seen how they've stuck beside the team through multiple years of losing seasons and the breakthrough when they finally cracked the postseason after a 16-year drought.

Christie's message to the fans: "it won't always be like this."

"This is a process that we're going through to try to get to where we want to go, and their loyalty means everything," Christie told USA TODAY. " When I see them around town, they're always (saying) 'coach keep going, keep pushing,' and that's what I do every day. I'll always be the first one in the building, working until we figure this thing out."

Kings forward Keegan Murray had a similar message to the fans to keep supporting, despite the shortcomings.

"I love our fans. They've been great to us... to me. I appreciate them coming out to support, we know that Rome's not built in a day but at the end of the day we're trying," Murray told USA TODAY. "With their support, it'll only get better."

Murray, Sabonis and Monk are the few Kings players that have been around for their lone playoff appearance in the last 15 years. Murray often tells the team, especially Acuff who was down in the dumps after a recent home loss, about how loud Golden 1 Center can get when their team is rolling.

"When we're really good, this place is better than any arena in the NBA," Murray said. "I feel like that's a big motivating factor in what we're trying to get to. ... I'm just hoping we can get back on track."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

#2766. Jerry Jones: "I don't think we're far away" from 18 regular-season games

As the NFL embarks on the second half of its current 18-week regular-season schedule, it’s just a matter of time before the current structure changes.

It’s no secret that the NFL wants to expand the regular season from 17 to 18 games. The league is sufficiently confident about it happening that folks like Cowboys owner Jerry Jones speak of it as a given.

“I don’t think we’re far away from it,” Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, regarding the addition of an extra game. “I don’t know how — what is far away. Next month? No. Next year? Maybe. [The] next year? Maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players.

“But it’s in everybody’s best interests.  You’d cut back on the preseason games. You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason. But it’s in everybody’s interest, and it certainly is in the players’ best interest in my mind, for sure.  And having said that, I would anticipate that coming.”

His comments presume the NFL Players Association will happily agree to 18 regular-season games. They likely won’t. At a minimum, they’ll seek major concessions in exchange for the willingness to add yet another game that counts.

The unspoken goal had been 2027. The NFL delayed picking a date for Super Bowl LXII in Atlanta in order to accommodate the possibility that the game will slide a week or two deeper into February. That would make 2028 the earliest year for expansion, as a practical matter. (Adding a game for 2027 would be possible only if the dead week between the conference championships is wiped out or if the season starts a week earlier. If an 18th game will result in a second bye, both would be required.)

Expansion by 2027 would require expedited negotiations. Expansion by 2028 would hinge on the NFL and NFLPA striking a deal within the next year or so. The union has shown no inclination, however, to engage in talks aimed at extending the current Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season.

Still, if push comes to shove, there will be 18 games. The blueprint was created in 2011. The NFL will lock the players out until the players agree to the things the owners want. Most notably, 18 regular-season games and 16 annual international games.

Beyond that, Jones’s comment about the early games of the season is odd. “You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason.”

He says that as if it’s a good thing. It definitely is not. Already, teams struggle in September to get up to speed, given that most teams (with the exception of those assigned to the Hall of Fame Game) play only three preseason games. When the preseason reduces to two games, that’s even fewer chances to prepare.

It’s also fewer chances for the non-starters to get the attention of coaches and General Managers in games that don’t count in the standings. It will become harder for undrafted free agents to make the 53-man rosters.

Regardless, the motivation isn’t football. It’s money. More inventory equals more weekends equals more broadcast windows equals more revenue.

And that likely will continue until the preseason shrinks to zero games — and the regular season expands to 20 games.

#2764. Sixers finding success manufacturing their own energy

It was only the first quarter of the 13th game of the Sixers' season, so there seemed to be no cause for alarm (and never mind the booing). Still, they were down 17 to a Toronto team on the second half of a back-to-back and playing without its two best players. There was at least the possibility Thursday that it was one of those nights every NBA team has on occasion, where the mood and the energy and the desire are just … off.

It would be easy to reach that conclusion, after Boston smacked the Sixers around Tuesday, in what was supposed to be the Jaylen Brown Revenge Game. Also, LeBron James sat out against the Raptors. The official reason was "low back/sciatica management," though this seems comparable to that time years ago when the Spurs rested Tim Duncan and listed him this way in the boxscore: "DNP-OLD."

When Nick Nurse called timeout with 2:40 left in the first and his team down 32-16, he said he was thinking in the simplest terms.

"I just want the players to play well," he said, adding that everyone seemed to be searching for a rhythm, or seeking to "shake something off from the last game or whatever," as he put it.

They fell 17 back moments later, but soon found their inspiration, soon manufactured their own energy. Reserves Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker found it by looking back to their time on some wretched Portland teams. VJ Edgecombe found it by looking forward to a potential spot in the NBA slam-dunk contest.

And Tyrese Maxey found it by looking over to the sideline, to his infant daughter.

The end result was a 123-112 Sixers victory over the Scottie Barnes– and Kawhi Leonard-less Raptors. Maxey scored 27, and Joel Embiid, who limped off in the first quarter after bumping knees with a Raptor, returned and finished with 20. Edgecombe enjoyed a Swiss Army Knife kinda night – 15 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals and a block – and the bench brigade of Simons, Walker and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope contributed 37 points, including 9-for-12 three-point sniping.

"You learn once you're coming off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said after going 5-for-6 from the arc and scoring 17.

What he read before checking in at the aforementioned timeout was straight out of the Stephen King collection. So the idea, Simons said, was to "bring some energy and some life to the team."

He provided the night's first thunderbolt, nailing a three-ball at the first-period buzzer to cut the deficit to nine.

"Those are big momentum plays," Nurse said, "that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment."

From that point forward, the Sixers, now 10-3, seemed inevitable. Edgecombe turned a second-quarter steal into a breakaway slam. Maxey threw an alley-oop to Brown from midcourt for a bucket late in the third, when Philadelphia went ahead for good. And with the Raptors hanging around late in the fourth, Simons and Caldwell-Pope (11 points) connected from three to put it away.

Re Simons: Now in his ninth NBA season, he is playing for his fourth team. He has been productive everywhere he's been, but this year his minutes (21.7) and points (10.2) are down from their usual levels. He says he doesn't care – not after playing on losing teams five of the seven seasons he spent in Portland, his first stop. The Blazers were 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46 the last three of those seasons, when Walker was a teammate. (Another Sixer, Rayan Rupert, was on two of those teams.)

"You learn a lot in those situations about yourself, the people around you, your teammates," Simons said, adding that "you feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning. And so that's something that you can't take for granted for sure, because it's hard to win in the NBA."

Sometimes it's hard to even get on the court, as Walker has learned. He is averaging 15 minutes a game over five seasons, but now looms as the best option to back up Embiid at center, despite standing 6-7. Not to worry, he said after contributing nine points and eight boards in just under 16 minutes Thursday; his dad, Samaki, had been a small-ball center himself while playing a decade in the Association. The younger Walker knows the assignment, knows what the job entails.

He's also healthy this season, having undergone offseason knee surgery. And while it wasn't clear where he might fit in the pecking order after the Sixers revamped their roster over the summer, he had high hopes.

"I don't know if I was delusional," he said, "but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part. I read some things, and they say it's a surprise. But if you were around me this summer and saw the mindset I had, then it wouldn't be a surprise. So this is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

There were also questions about Edgecombe's role coming into the season. But his attitude is always exemplary, his approach relentless. Informed after Thursday's game that the only guard in the league with more dunks than him was Houston's Amen Thompson, he scoffed.

"Man, he don't even count," Edgecombe said.

He might have a point. Thompson stands 6-7. Edgecombe is listed at 6-4, but attacks the rim so regularly that he is musing about the dunk contest on All-Star Weekend, February in Phoenix.

"Obviously I don't want to sit here and give a yes, and I don't want to give a no," he said. "But that's something I'm thinking about, for sure."

Maxey couldn't help but think about his daughter Marvel. Born May 14 to Tyrese and his girlfriend Myra Gordon, she attended her first game with her mom Thursday – "a really cool moment," as Maxey said.

She might not be back for a while, though.

"It's too late," he said. "She was yawning and doing a whole bunch of stuff."

So too were the Sixers for a while. They awakened from their slumber. They found their footing, manufactured their own energy. On many, many nights across the long season, that's how it has to be.

#2762. Ground stop results in side judge Don Willard serving as referee for two games on Sunday

Friday’s nationwide ground stop won’t keep NFL teams from getting to their road games on Sunday. It will, however, impact the ability of officials to get to where they need to be.

The NFL has announced that officiating assignments have changed for Week 10. And the situation will result in a backup referee serving as the referee in two games on the same day.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” the NFL said in a statement. “The changes will necessitate that three backup referees — umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard [pictured] — will work as referees in the following games: Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt; Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson; Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati – Don Willard.

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise.”

The situation creates the likely unprecedented situation of a referee working two games in one day. Willard will handle Dolphins-Colts at 1:00 p.m. ET, and then he’ll make the 109-mile trip from Indianapolis to Cincinnati for the Sunday night game.

Making the unprecedented even more unusual is the fact that Willard’s usual crew (led by referee Scott Novak) wasn’t scheduled to work at all this weekend.

The announcement doesn’t address where the referees for those three games will be working, or what their roles will be. Shawn Smith was scheduled to be the referee for Panthers-Saints, Alex Moore was set to be the referee for Jaguars-Titans, Carl Cheffers was due to be the referee for Dolphins-Colts, and Clete Blakeman was slated to be the referee for Steelers-Bengals.

The league’s statement also doesn’t specify other shifts that were required as to the established crews that work together throughout the regular season.

#2760. International player Joshua Weru on his development behind the scenes

International player Joshua Weru on his development behind the scenes originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Joshua Weru was the talk of training camp this summer. While draft pick Uar Bernard grabbed headlines this spring, it was the Eagles' other International Player Pathway Program player who began to stand out in August.

The edge rusher from Kenya flashed in practices and even in the preseason a bit — to the point where some worried he'd be claimed if the Eagles dared to waive him to get him to the practice squad.

But that was months ago and now we're in November.

Weru has spent all season on the Eagles' practice squad. And most days this season, Weru walks through the Eagles locker room mostly unnoticed. He'll sit at his locker without being bothered and hadn't really been asked for an interview all season. Until last week. So Weru seemed a bit surprised when he was approached and asked for a few minutes, which he graciously handed over.

What have the last couple of months been like?

"It's been good," Weru said. "I continue to say I'm so lucky to be here. The amount of reps we get on scout team and developmental have been good. Just seeing things better and recognizing blocks quicker. Just getting my strike stronger. Even though I'm not necessarily getting stronger in the weight room, like actual game strength is getting slightly better. Just those things because you're more used to doing certain movements so you're getting better at it."

Weru, 23, hasn't been elevated yet this season so he hasn't played in a game since the preseason. Weru misses playing, but last week invoked the old proverb — absence makes the heart grow fonder — to explain his situation.

Over the last couple months, Weru knows he has gotten better. Although he's unsure how to quantify it, his growth is undeniable.

Away from the spotlight of training camp, Weru has settled into a rhythm as a practice squad player. Tuesdays are big for him to get in extra voluntary work. And then on days the Eagles practice, he goes out early to get in what Nick Sirianni always calls "500 shots" of extra work. Those extra sessions for Weru and fellow rookie Keyshawn James-Newby are run by outside linebackers coach Jeremiah Washburn and assistant linebackers coach Tyler Scudder.

But a big part of Weru's role as a special teams player is contributing on the scout team. So each week, he dons a pinny and tries to give the Eagles' offensive line the best looks he can for that upcoming game.

Jordan Mailata has seen a lot of Weru on the scout team this season and admitted the rookie got under his skin a little bit to end last week: "He's very fast and twitchy so he gave a great look this week."

Mailata admitted that because of Weru's lack of football knowledge, misdirections will fool him to where he'll over commit or lose contain in the run game. But Mailata has already seen Weru improve in those areas week by week.

"He's going through that but he's doing a great job of not taking that too personal," Mailata said. "He's hard on himself a good amount. His effort is greater than mine ever was. I just saw him chase down Saquon (Barkley) it was incredible. Incredible."

Weru takes pride in his job as a scout team player and keeps a close eye on the Eagles' offensive linemen on Sunday.

"That gets me fired up, getting to watch them," Weru said. "If I see that they've been doing well, I feel like I helped a bit at least."

The interesting part of being a scout team player for someone like Weru, who hasn't been playing football for very long, is that it exposes him to other styles of defense. This year on scout team, Weru has been learning how to play out of three-point and four-point stances, which has taken some getting used to.

Weru said he didn't realize how hard it would be to get out of a stance like that.

"I feel like I'm slowly getting better at that," he said. "It's also helped me get more reactive because it's not playing to the rules that we have. So you kind of have to know what's going on."

Weru has been practicing every week, while his fellow IPP teammate, Bernard, has been on the Practice Squad Injured List since Oct. 9.

Bernard and Weru were big stories back in training camp and many wondered if they would make the 53-man roster and feared if they didn't, another team would scoop them up. But both players were cut, cleared waivers and immediately signed to the Eagles' practice squad.

While Weru obviously wanted to make the Eagles' roster, he never wanted to leave. And now that he's away from the spotlight a bit, he has been able to grow each week behind the scenes.

No one really knows what the future holds for Weru. Even though the Eagles once hit it big on an IPP player in Mailata, the odds are stacked against Weru and Bernard. But there's no harm in trying and Weru has continued to put in the work.

"It's been really good because just growing and building relationships with guys in my room, coaches, the development staff, all my teammates," Weru said. "So I just feel increasingly comfortable. I can see how much time they're willing to invest in me. I'm just happy to be here."

#2759. Report: Vikings first reached out to Raiders about Kirk Cousins on "midday Monday"

As it turns out, the Vikings contacted the Raiders about a possible trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins before Monday night’s meltdown from quarterback Carson Wentz.

Via ESPNFL, the Vikings initially contacted the Raiders during “midday Monday,” prior to Minnesota’s Week 9 game against the Bills. The Vikings told the Raiders they wanted to see how things went during the Monday night game before having any further conversations.

Then came Wentz’s 8.9-passer rating performance in a 23-6 loss, and Minnesota mobilized. The Vikings, per the report, contacted the Raiders before 6:00 a.m. PT on Tuesday and commenced the talks that culminated in a deal being done.

Said Raiders G.M. John Spytek during a Tuesday press conference: “I never made one call on Kirk Cousins. And I got a few phone calls. But one real one this morning.”

The Vikings initially offered a fifth-round pick for Cousins, per the report. The report doesn’t specify the Raiders’ opening position.

Once the Vikings moved to a third-round pick, the Raiders pounced.

Beyond avoiding the $10 million guaranteed bonus and clearing the path for rookie No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza (which are mentioned in the article), the Raiders ultimately bought a third-round pick for $650,000 (which is not).

That’s the most attractive aspect of the entire transaction, in our view. Nearly 10 years ago, the Browns bought a second-round pick from the Texans by assuming quarterback Brock Osweiler’s $16 million full guarantee for the 2017 season. Any team would sprint for the chance to purchase a third-round pick in the 2027 draft for only $650,000.

In this case, that bargain came with nine starts from Cousins, four wins, and months of excellent mentorship for Mendoza.

As to the lingering sense in some circles that the Raiders could have gotten even more for Cousins, they risked driving a bargain so hard that the Vikings would have walked away and made a trade with another team.

So it was a win for the Vikings, who got their first choice. It was a win for the Raiders. And it definitely was a win for Cousins, who went from waiting to be benched for Mendoza to having nine games as the starter for a contender — plus the strong possibility that the Vikings will make the playoffs.

#2756. Future Eagles Fits: Jeremiah Smith headlines an explosive 2027 WR class

Future Eagles Fits: Jeremiah Smith headlines an explosive 2027 WR class originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Welcome back to Future Eagles Fits, our weekly deep dive into the prospects who could eventually find their way to Philadelphia.

Every week, we're going inside the tape and looking at prospects through an Eagles-centric lens — breaking down the athletic profile, positional versatility and scheme fit that could ultimately determine whether a player makes sense in Philly. Along the way, we'll examine how prospects are being evaluated across the league as draft boards begin to take shape and conversations are had with representatives across the scouting landscape.

For the Eagles, it's been a mixed bag on the outside this fall. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks have missed significant time, Darius Cooper has shown some flashes albeit in small spurts, but rookie Makai Lemon, who currently leads the team in targets, receptions and receiving yards through the first nine weeks of the season, has done an excellent job all things considered. The first-year wideout has been a focal point in the offense and looks like a legitimate complementary WR2 moving forward. Still, however, there are questions about the overall composition of the group and whether Philly has enough explosiveness on the outside to consistently threaten defenses at all three levels. You know what Smith offers, and Lemon has provided a reliable presence, but adding another dynamic playmaker with the ability to create separation, stretch the field and generate yards after the catch could give this offense another dimension.

Currently, the Eagles hold the fifth overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, along with the 25th overall pick following the trade of Jordan Davis to Jacksonville. That gives Howie Roseman unique flexibility at the top of the draft, particularly if Philadelphia wants to make another significant investment in the receiver position after drafting Lemon on Night 1 last spring. Whether it's targeting a potential franchise-caliber weapon with an early first-round selection or finding another explosive playmaker later in the round, there are several intriguing options to consider.

While there is still a ton of football left to be played and the entirety of the pre-draft process still to play out – which will alter draft boards – here are six pass-catchers to know in the upcoming class — two potential Day 1 targets, two Day 2 prospects and two Day 3 options who could provide some pop on the outside.

Day 1: Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State | 6'3″, 225 lbs, estimated 4.43 40 time (via summer testing)

If the Eagles are fortunate enough to have Jeremiah Smith available with the fifth overall selection, sprint the card up to the podium.

Simply put, Smith is as elite a wide receiver prospect that the NFL has seen since the likes of Julio Jones coming out of Alabama years ago. A "potential All-Pro as a rookie" as a source said, his combination of size, physicality, and explosiveness is as impressive as you'll find at the position in this draft class, or any other. At 6-foot-3, he has the ability to overwhelm defensive backs physically while maintaining the athleticism and explosiveness to separate at the top of routes, the strength to consistently win through contact and the type of ball skills that allow him to make plays far outside his frame hauling in passes like a Venus flytrap above the helmet of opposing corners.

A former five-star recruit and Heisman trophy candidate this fall, what separates Smith from other physically imposing receivers in the past is his ability to dominate at all three levels of an offense. He's not simply a big-bodied possession receiver who wins in the red zone. He can threaten defenses vertically, create separation on intermediate routes, and turn underneath opportunities into explosive gains with his ability to run through contact and generate yards after the catch.

There's also a level of polish to his game that makes his evaluation particularly exciting. Smith has the physical tools to dominate NFL corners immediately, but he's also shown the ability to consistently win in different situations and against different coverage looks. He's the type of receiver who doesn't need a perfect quarterback situation to produce, making him about as close to a quarterback-proof offensive weapon as you'll find. Quite frankly, he's a player who could have made the jump to the NFL a couple of years ago and still been one of the more talented receivers in the league. He's that special of a talent.

For the Eagles, Smith would represent an opportunity to add a legitimate cornerstone piece to the offensive skill group and showcase what would be arguably the NFL's top wide receiver tandem alongside DeVonta Smith. With questions surrounding the long-term composition of the receiver room and the potential need for another dominant outside presence, his ability to win vertically, create after the catch and consistently command attention from opposing defenses would immediately change the way teams have to defend the Eagles. If he's available at No. 5, no matter what your depth chart looks like, you turn in his card and don't think twice. He's the top player in the 2027 class.

Day 1: Jackson Harris, LSU | 6'2″, 205 lbs, 4.45 estimated 40 time (via summer testing)

A transfer to Baton Rouge from Hawaii, Harris has gone from being a likely Day 3 pick to an athlete that will likely hear his name called on Night 1.

At his size, Harris brings an appealing combination of outstanding route-running and playmaking ability on the outside. He's a receiver with the type of frame NFL teams covet, particularly when evaluating players who can operate outside the numbers and give quarterbacks a legitimate target in contested situations. His transition to the SEC has been particularly impressive, and the production he's put together this season has helped elevate his draft stock. After announcing himself on the SEC stage in Week 4 with 195 receiving yards against Texas A&M, Harris is coming off of electric back-to-back performances against Auburn and Alabama to the tune of 21 catches for 359 yards and two TDs combined in the last two weeks. Defenses know the ball is going his way, and they still can't do anything about it.

For the Eagles, the 25th overall selection could be an interesting range to explore if Harris remains available. His size and ability to provide another outside presence would give the Eagles some additional flexibility with its personnel groupings.

Day 2: Deuce Alexander, Ole Miss | 5'11", 180 lbs, 4.33 estimated 40 time (via summer testing)

If you're looking for an explosive weapon who can immediately add a completely unique dimension to an offense, Alexander is the guy here on Day 2. A Wake Forest transfer, Alexander brings a completely different physical profile than some of the bigger-bodied receivers at the top of the board as his burst and top end speed will force opposing coordinators to know where he his on every snap.

He's not going to overwhelm defensive backs with size, but his fundamental explosiveness and ability to create separation are what make him such an interesting prospect. There are some similarities to Lions WR Jameson Williams in the way he moves and threatens defenses vertically, as Alexander has the type of acceleration and track speed that can force opposing defenses to respect the deep ball, while his ability to create separation gives him opportunities to make plays underneath, as well. He's the type of receiver who can force advantageous matchups for an offense simply by being on the field.

For the Eagles, Alexander would provide a different element to the receiver room. Philadelphia already has a few established options who can operate in the intermediate areas of the field, but adding another receiver with legitimate vertical speed could open up opportunities for the entire offense by forcing defenses to cover every single blade of grass. His ability to threaten defenses over the top and generate explosive plays would make him an appealing complementary piece, particularly if the Eagles are looking to add more speed without allocating first-round capital.

Day 2: Ryan Wingo, Texas | 6'1″, 214 lbs, 4.37 estimated 40 time (via summer testing)

Wingo is another receiver who makes just about everything look easy when watching the tape. Operating in Steve Sarkisian's offense at Texas, he's been utilized in a variety of ways, and that versatility is one of the more appealing aspects of his evaluation.

At 6-foot-1, Wingo has an impressive combination of size, strength and elite athleticism. He's a well-built receiver who can operate outside, but his skill set extends beyond simply lining up on the perimeter and running traditional route concepts. Texas has done an excellent job finding different ways to get him involved, whether that's through jet sweeps, the screen game, vertical opportunities or allowing him to create after the catch to showcase his track speed (as a former All-State sprinter during his prep years in Missouri).

His versatility is highly intriguing as he doesn't need a specific type of play call to make an impact. He's comfortable working with the ball in his hands, has the speed to threaten defenses vertically, and also possesses the physical profile to create problems when defensive backs attempt to tackle him in space. That alone is unique. He's the type of player who can provide an offense with multiple answers depending on the defensive personnel and coverage they're facing.

There's also something to be said about how naturally he operates within the offense. Wingo doesn't necessarily need to be force-fed opportunities to become an impact player, and his ability to contribute in different areas makes him an appealing evaluation for teams looking for more than just a traditional outside receiver.

For Philly, that versatility could be particularly valuable. The Eagles have continued to look for ways to create more explosive opportunities within its offensive structure, and Wingo would provide another player capable of contributing both on designed touches and as a legitimate downfield threat. His skillset expands a playbook.

Day 3: Cayden Lee, Missouri | 5'10", 175 lbs, 4.55 estimated 40 time (via summer testing)

Don't dismiss Lee because of his size, as his ability to consistently make plays regardless of the situation is what makes him worth monitoring. An Ole Miss transfer, Lee has established himself as one of the most productive receivers in the SEC and currently leads the conference in receiving yards with 835 through nine games.

At 5-foot-10, his game isn't predicated on overwhelming defensive backs physically. Instead, his game is built around nuance – the ability to consistently catch the football, mirroring similar routes, create separation and make plays beyond his frame. He has some of the best hands in the country and understands how to find openings in coverage and give his quarterback an opportunity to complete passes, and there's a level of consistency to his game that stands out when watching him. There are some similarities to Lemon in the way he operates as a receiver, as well. He's not the biggest, fastest, or most physically imposing player on the field, but his ability to consistently get involved, make difficult catches and produce within an offense showcases a heck of a football player.

The Eagles don't necessarily need another receiver who profiles as a traditional outside target, but finding a reliable player who can contribute as a WR4 or WR5 while providing some additional explosiveness to the offense potentially on special teams is never a bad investment. His ability to consistently make plays and his production against SEC competition make him a name worth keeping an eye on as the process unfolds.

Day 3: Justin Bowick, Oklahoma State | 6'3″, 203 lbs, 4.50 estimated 40 time (via summer testing)

Bowick is a name whose draft stock could continue trending upward as the evaluation process moves along. Playing at Oklahoma State and catching passes from Drew Mestemaker, potentially the first QB off the board in April, Bowick has an opportunity to continue building his profile as a big-bodied perimeter target.

At 6-foot-3, he brings a physical profile that immediately pops on tape. He's a large presence on the outside who can present matchup problems for opposing defensive backs, particularly when working in contested-catch situations and giving his quarterback a bigger window to throw into. His size alone makes him an interesting developmental prospect, especially for the Eagles who could eye another outside receiver who can provide a different physical element to their offense.

Right now, he has mid to late Day 3 grades from teams but is likely a player to fully indulge himself in the pre-draft process, meaning a good showing at an All-Star game (Senior Bowl or East-West Shrine), the NFL Combine, and pro day circuit could move him up boards significantly.

#2754. JJ Redick has lofty defensive identity for Lakers: ‘Physical as f–k’

We all know JJ Redick is a basketball sicko.

You know, the type of guy who rewatches games in a dark basement to pore over what he and the Lakers could've done better.

On Friday, we got a glimpse of what his staff is doing behind the scenes.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on during the first half of an NBA basketball game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Nov. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Aaron Gash

Redick said his analytics team used the three-day break between games to prepare a 21-page presentation on the Lakers, who have won seven games in a row and have the NBA's best record at 11-2.

The coaches reviewed it for 1 ½ hours on Friday and presented it to the players.

"Being first in the West, with the stuff that they showed us, you would think we were almost last, you know?" Ziaire Williams said, flashing a smile. "But gotta keep us honest."

"We know we want to be a top-10 defense," Redick said. "We know we are not going to be able to do that unless we become better than a bottom-10 transition team and better than a bottom-10 defensive rebounding team."

While the Lakers are leading the league in steals per game (11), are third in blocks per game (6.2) and are second in total deflections (257), they're greatly struggling in other areas defensively.

The Lakers are rated 18th defensively and 26th in rebounding (40.8).

Redick also identified a key area on transition defense he wants to tweak.

"Some of the transition stuff is live-ball turnovers," Redick said. "We're at a 10% live-ball turnover rate. So one out of every 10 possessions is a live-ball turnover that's going to create a transition possession."

Despite being the top-rated team in the league offensively, the Lakers have multiple areas in which they want to improve, including bolstering their third unit, which has notoriously squandered leads late in games.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick and Luka Doncic converse with referee James Williams during a game against the Atlanta Hawks on Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

Redick pointed out that Cameron Carr and Adou Thiero are still playing catch-up after missing time due to various injuries.

Lakers assistant coach Scott Brooks is trying to get them up to speed.

"He took those guys for a classroom setting [Friday]," Redick said. "We just need to coach them more. Not going to put it all on them. They need to be able to run offense, though.

"I think that's the biggest thing. It's unacceptable to just consistently be calling offensive plays and then they come down and jack a 3 with 18 on the shot clock. We're trying to use time and be organized."

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick reacts on the sidelines during a game against the Atlanta Hawks in Atlanta on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Redick, whom the Lakers hired to take over the helm in June 2024 despite having no prior coaching experience, has shined in his role.

He led the Lakers to back-to-back 50-win seasons for the first time since Phil Jackson in 2007-2011.

He has a clear idea of what he wants the Lakers' identity to be on both sides of the court.

"Organized, unselfish and advantage-based," he said.

"Organized, physical as f–k and relentless," he added.

#2752. Bob Stoops challenges Oklahoma fans ahead of Sunday's game

The Oklahoma Sooners have had a wild last few days. The Sooners were originally scheduled to play the Ole Miss Rebels on Saturday at 3:15 p.m. CT; however, due to the FAA grounding all flights and the Rebels saying they couldn't travel until Saturday afternoon, even though the grounding was lifted Friday night, the game was pushed to Sunday at noon.

This caused a lot of outrage among Oklahoma fans, as they felt they were being punished despite Ole Miss' inept planning. On top of that, a cold front and storm are predicted to move through the area, with temperatures forecast to be in the 40s and a high chance of rain on Sunday during the game.

This led legendary former Oklahoma head coach Bob Stoops to urge Sooner fans to show up and create a miserable atmosphere for the visiting Rebels.

"Okay, Sooner fans, even though every other college football game is being played (Saturday), our game will be Sunday at noon," Stoops said on X. "So, it's time to flip the script. Let's all dress for the weather and show up for our team. If you're unable to attend the game, please give your tickets to someone who can. I'm throwing down the challenge to all Sooner Nation. Let's answer the call and be the loudest, proudest, most raucous crowd we've been all year. Let's bring the energy. Bring the noise and remind Ole Miss exactly who they're playing. Boomer Sooner."

Stoops' message gives Oklahoma fans a chance to turn an unusual and frustrating weekend into an opportunity to make their presence felt. The schedule change and unfavorable weather could make Sunday's atmosphere different from anything the Sooners have experienced this season, but the former head coach believes the fan base can use that to its advantage. With kickoff moved to noon and rain potentially in the forecast, showing up and bringing energy will be especially important.

The Sooners will need that support against an Ole Miss team still fighting for its postseason hopes. Oklahoma has an opportunity to defend its home field and pick up a big SEC win, but the focus must remain on executing between the lines. If Sooner fans answer Stoops' challenge, the Rebels could face an intimidating environment despite the unusual Sunday kickoff. As Stoops made clear, he wants the entire fan base to make sure Ole Miss knows exactly what awaits in Norman.

#2750. Why was Jordan Davis listening to Sinatra on his way out of Philly?

Why was Jordan Davis listening to Sinatra on his way out of Philly? originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The trade came as a shock to Jordan Davis, so on the way to the airport he did the only thing that made sense.

"On the way to the airport in Philly, I had a moment," Davis said. "You know, I try not to cry. But I prayed and I played a song, Frank Sinatra, My Way.And I think that just encompasses (my) time there and just stepping away and looking toward a new future.

"And obviously the time that I spent in Philly, I have grown so much from that. And I became a better player because of it, became a better man because of it. And it's not to say that I would ever sit there and turn my back on Philly. I don't have any hate. I don't have any bad blood against it. It's just the business of it all. It's just the nature of the beast. And I'm grateful for the time. But right now, I have another mission. I have a new city to embrace.

"Excited to give back to the community and get into the community and see what all Jacksonville has to offer. So I guess I'll save that for retirement. When I really do the big big cry."

Davis spoke to Jacksonville media on Wednesday and clips from that interview were posted on social media by Action Sports Jacksonville, which is Jacksonville's CBS47 and Fox30.

The Eagles traded Davis, their 2022 1st-round pick, to the Jaguars Monday for a 1st-round pick in 2027 and a 2nd-round pick in 2029.

"Excited to work," Davis said. "We have a good front, so excited to be a piece of it. I'm just optimistic about the future. I'm optimistic about me playing a role and being who I am and being a piece to add to this already good team. And however far that we go, I hope to be a part of it."

Davis was a four-year starter with the Eagles, a starter on two Super Bowl teams, a champion in 2024 and a key figure on the NFL's No.1 defense. He had a Pro Bowl-caliber season in 2025 but his play dropped off in the nine games he played for the Eagles this year before the trade.

Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said in a Zoom call with Jaguars media he believes defensive tackles in general can continue to improve well into their career and thinks Davis still has plenty of up-side."That was a major piece to the puzzle," he said. "It's a position that ages well, and certainly look forward to seeing him integrate here in the early going, while at the same time knowing that it's going to be a longer-term decision that we made with him.

"And so making sure that his development over these next few years is something we really think through and plan out. But I think that's certainly a big piece to the why behind it."

With the trade, Davis went from last place to first place, from two wins to six wins. And he went from the NFL's No. 19 scoring defense to No. 2.

And if the Jags' defense seems a little familiar it's because defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile was Vic Fangio's linebackers coach with the Dolphins in 2023 and runs a lot of similar stuff.

"I'm here to do whatever the coaches need me to do," Davis said. "Still figuring out a plan, still learning the playbook. … It's easy to learn. It's different languages. The structure is the same as coming from Philly. The defensive structure is the same. It's the same tree. But it's just learning the language, learning the little nuances of the play.

"It's a lot more fronts that they play here than they did in Philly with a little bit of effort (on the) grindstone, and I'll be here a little bit later (Wednesday) night, I'll pick it up soon."

Jaguars coach Liam Coen recalled coaching against Davis in college and just being struck by his size.

"Jordan Davis, competed against and coached against him when he was at Georgia in 2021 when I was at Kentucky," he said. "And I just remember him walking the field pregame and I'm wondering how we're gonna gain a yard with that defense they had there.

"A young ascending player that has a lot of freakish traits. I mean, he's a large human being that can move, that does have some rush and some three-down value."

Davis joins a terrific defensive line that also includes Georgia teammate Travon Walker, the first pick in the 2022 draft that also produced Davis at No. 13 overall.

"It's gonna be great having my brother back with me," Walker said in another Action Sports video. "If you look back at the season he had last year and the season that he's going to put together this year, obviously, he's still potentially is going to grow every day and that's something that we always preach on there, at Georgia and I'm pretty sure his coaches (with the Eagles) preached on that really as well and now, he's here. So now coach is pretty saying the same thing every day. He wants to get better every day."

The Jaguars on Monday also acquired safety Jessie Bates from the Falcons and defensive tackle Davon Godchaux from the Saints as they reshaped their defense for the stretch run.

"I'm a big guy too, but Jordan, he's huge," Godchaux said. "I'm excited to play with him, feed off him, him feed off me. It's gonna be special. We've got a great group of guys who were already here before we got here. So we're all gonna come together. But, I mean, we have a great group on paper. We still gotta go out and prove it each and every week."

Davis leaves a team that's lost seven straight games and joins a team that on Sunday will be going for its sixth win in seven games. The Jags face the Titans in Nashville Sunday afternoon. The Jags already had their bye so Davis could play 18 games this year.

"I think anybody who plays in big games has a certain level of experience that they could bring to another level," Davis said. "It takes a lot to go to the Super Bowl and it takes a lot to win a Super Bowl, but. right now we're in the process of just one game at a time.

"I know everybody likes to look to the end goal, but you can't see at the end if you don't see where your feet are right now. So I'm just enjoying it, enjoying the moment, looking for my first dub as a Jag, hopefully this weekend. We'll figure out where it goes at the end."

#2746. Eagles continue reshaping roster by reportedly releasing veteran wide receiver

Eagles continue reshaping roster by reportedly releasing veteran wide receiver originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Hollywood Brown's brief and odd Eagles career is over after four games and five catches.

The Eagles are releasing Brown by mutual consent of the player and the team, Jordan Schultz of the Scultz Report posted on social media Thursday night.

The Eagles signed Brown to a one-year, $5 million contract in March with the expectation that he'd be a significant part of the Eagles' passing game following the departure of A.J. Brown. But even with Brown gone and DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks both hurt much of the season, Brown has been an afterthought.

He's only played in four of the Eagles' nine games, getting nine targets and catching five passes for 63 yards along with two rushing attempts for 12 yards. His longest catch was a 19-yarder from Tanner McKee in the loss to the Cowboys. He had a season-high 30 yards in that game.

Brown expressed frustration with his limited role in a recent conversation with NBC Sports Philadelphia:

"Of course, you want to be somewhere where you play, but at the ultimate end of the day, it's not my plan. So I might want to play, I might want to contribute, but if that's not the plan for me, I can't dwell on it too much or you'll be unhappy. And then you're taking that back home. I can't take that back home to the wife and kids. So I gotta try to stay as positive as I can."

Asked how that was going, he laughed and said, "Some days better than others."

He added: "We're all dealing with something and we're dealing with something as a team. So I don't wanna add that extra stress."

Brown said he expected to play more but was dealing with it because he didn't want to put personal issues ahead of team needs.

"I did (expect a bigger role), but I do understand stuff happens," he said. "I mean, you can't take anything personal in this business, so you kind of just got to go about your process and when that time happens, whatever happens, you've just got to be ready for it."

Brown, a 1st-round pick in 2019, had a 1,000-yard season for the Ravens in 2021 and over 700 yards in both 2020 and 2022. He was 49-for-587 with five touchdowns last year. In his career, he has 378 catches for 4,385 yards and 33 touchdowns.

The Eagles, 2-7, have lost seven straight game. Their offense is ranked 32nd in the NFL in yards per game, 30th in points per game and 29th in passing yards per game.

With Brown no longer on the roster, the Eagles have rookie 1st-round pick Makai Lemon, 2nd-year undrafted free agent Darius Cooper and Elijah Moore as healthy wide receivers. Smith and Wicks have both missed the last two games but could be back after the bye week.

Lemon is the Eagles' leading receiver with 37-for-312 and a touchdown and Smith (26-310-2), Wicks (19-284-1) and Cooper (13-200-4) are next.

The Eagles have two WRs on the practice squad – Erik Ezukanma and Xavier Gipson.

Because it's after the trade deadline, Brown is subject to the waiver claim process despite being a vested veteran with seven years of pension credit.

#2745. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

Pollard is in the final year of a three-year, $21.75 million contract. He’s due to be a free agent in March.

#2743. The Suns are getting crushed in one critical area of the game

When you look at the Phoenix Suns and see a 5-6 record staring back at you, there are plenty of explanations for why they've stumbled out of the gate. One of the most obvious is the schedule. According to ESPN's strength-of-schedule metrics, Phoenix has faced the third-toughest slate in the NBA through the first 11 games of the season. We can also point to the ongoing challenges surrounding Jalen Green and his inability to consistently find his place on this roster. We can discuss how Miles Bridges has yet to hit his stride as he continues adjusting to a new team, a new system, and new responsibilities.

But there's one glaring deficiency that threatens to haunt the Suns throughout the entire season unless they fundamentally change their approach or somehow miraculously become a larger basketball team overnight. Their inability to impact the game at the rim. And the numbers are downright horrific.

Last season, Phoenix finished 29th in the NBA in field goal attempts within five feet of the basket, averaging 23.7 per game. This season? They're averaging 23.5, the fifth fewest in the league. Think about that for a moment. The Suns have a healthy Jalen Green, a player whose athleticism and explosiveness theoretically provide the ability to get downhill and attack the basket. They also brought in Miles Bridges, another player expected to provide a more physical presence and generate opportunities around the rim. And through 11 games, neither addition has meaningfully moved the needle. Phoenix is attacking the basket at essentially the same rate as last season, despite investing significant resources in players who were supposed to address that very deficiency.

But the offensive struggles around the cylinder are only half the problem. The other half? Rebounding. And somehow, the numbers are even uglier.

The Suns rank dead last in the NBA in rebounds per game, averaging a miserable 38.9. That's a full 10 rebounds fewer than the Minnesota Timberwolves, who lead the league at 48.9 per game. Phoenix also ranks 30th in rebounding percentage at 45.2%, meaning opponents are consistently winning the battle for available rebounds.

When you begin examining how that translates into actual points, the situation becomes even more alarming. The Suns surrender 18.1 second-chance points per game, the second most in the league. Meanwhile, they're generating only 12.8 second-chance points themselves, the second fewest. So not only are opponents getting additional opportunities to score, but Phoenix is failing to create those same opportunities on the other end. That's a pretty brutal combination.

If you need a recent example of how dire the situation has become, look no further than Thursday night's victory over Charlotte. Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach, two of the players Phoenix relies upon to provide some semblance of interior presence, combined for five rebounds. In a game where the Suns were outrebounded by 21.

No matter how you slice it, this is a five-alarm fire for a team attempting to establish itself as a legitimate competitor in the Western Conference. Much like speed, size can't be taught. You can preach positioning, emphasize boxing out, and demand greater effort on the glass, but there's only so much coaching can accomplish when your roster consistently finds itself at a physical disadvantage.

The most deflating aspect of this deficiency is how it impacts both ends of the floor. Defensively, the Suns can execute an entire possession correctly, rotate effectively, contest shots, and force opponents into difficult attempts. But if they can't secure the rebound, all that work becomes meaningless. The possession continues, the defense has to scramble again, and another opportunity is handed to the opposition. You cannot consistently give NBA teams extra possessions and expect to win basketball games. It places an enormous burden on your defense, especially when you're already asking players to compensate for a lack of size and interior physicality.

And offensively, the inability to consistently attack and finish around the basket creates an entirely different set of problems. When opposing defenses don't have to respect your ability to penetrate and score at the rim, they can become more aggressive on the perimeter. They can close out harder, pressure ball handlers, and force you into difficult jump shots because they aren't particularly concerned about what happens if you get past the initial defender. Perhaps that also helps explain why Phoenix is averaging the second-fewest free throw attempts per game in the NBA. They're not getting to the rack.

It's an unsustainable combination of deficiencies, particularly for a team that doesn't possess the overwhelming offensive firepower to compensate for them. The Suns can survive a difficult schedule. They can work through the growing pains associated with integrating new players. They can experiment with rotations, redefine responsibilities, and hope that chemistry improves as the season progresses. But how exactly do you overcome being one of the worst teams in basketball at attacking the rim, rebounding the basketball, and preventing opponents from generating second-chance opportunities?

That's a much more difficult question to answer. And right now, I'm not sure the Phoenix Suns have one.

I'm trying to find a little optimism in all of this. The Suns are 5-6, they've played one of the toughest schedules in the league, and they have plenty of areas that need improvement. But we're still early enough in the season for adjustments to matter. Jalen Green can find his footing. Miles Bridges can become more comfortable in his role. The coaching staff can experiment with lineups and find better ways to generate opportunities around the basket.

None of that is guaranteed to solve the rebounding problem, and the lack of size remains a legitimate concern. But this team doesn't need to become a dominant interior force overnight. It needs to become more competitive in the areas that are currently costing it possessions and points. If Phoenix can make even modest progress there, there's still plenty of season left to build something worthwhile. The problems are real, but so is the opportunity to get better.

#2740. Warning to NFL general managers: Howie Roseman is about to fleece you

Warning to NFL general managers: Howie Roseman is about to fleece you originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

A broken-down receiver, a washed-up guard and an underachieving defensive tackle walk into a bar. And Howie Roseman walks out with two 1st-round picks and three 2nd-round picks.

If I were an NFL general manager, I wouldn't even answer the phone when Howie calls. Because you're going to get fleeced.

And if there's one thing to feel good about during this miserable season to nowhere, it's the way Howie has stockpiled premium draft picks with a series of what sure seem like lopsided trades.

It all started in June when Roseman shipped disgruntled and divisive A.J. Brown to the Patriots for a 1st-round pick in 2027 and a 5th-round pick in 2027.

Brown was one of the best in the league not too long ago. He owns the two-best receiving seasons in Eagles history – 88-for-1,496 and 11 TDs in 2022 and 106-for-1,456-7 in 2023.

But it sure seems like his knees won't allow him to be that kind of player again. The A.J. Brown we saw hobbling around and dropping passes in his final game in an Eagles uniform, the playoff loss to the 49ers in January, seems to be closer to the player he is now than the Pro Bowler of a few years ago.

The Patriots got a WR whose balky knees have allowed him to play only three games so far this year, with just nine catches for 101 yards, three drops and a fumble.

Of 95 WRs who've been targetted at least 20 times so far this year, Brown's 15 percent drop percentage is highest. And his catch percentage is 89th. Maybe he gets healthy the second half of the season and reverts back to that three-time Pro Bowler. Or maybe this is just who A.J. Brown is right now. Either way the Eagles got a 1st-round pick for a guy who had no future in Philadelphia, didn't want to be here and may be a shot fighter at 29.

Then came the Cam Jurgens trade, and it's still hard to believe the Ravens donated the Eagles a 2nd-round pick for a guy who just hasn't been the same player as he was in 2024. Jurgens was a tremendous interior lineman before his career was derailed by injuries. Although he made a second straight Pro Bowl last year, he was only a shell of the player he was in 2023 and 2024. This year, he struggled both at center and guard before Howie someone finagled a 2nd-round pick out of the Ravens for him.

How has it gone in Baltimore for Jurgens? You always take Pro Football Focus grades with a grain of salt, but out of 89 interior linemen who've played at least 300 snaps his 43.9 combined grade with the Eagles and Ravens is 4th-worst.

In Jurgens' three games in Baltimore, the Ravens – with both Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley hurt – have scored 33 points, gone 0-3, losing 35-13 to the Bengals, 36-10 to the Bills and 33-10 to the Jaguars after starting the season 4-1.

Then there's Jordan Davis. He was a good player here and at times a very good player. He probably should have made the Pro Bowl last year. But overall? As the 13th pick in the 2022 draft and the 10th-highest paid interior lineman in the league? He's underachieved, in particular this year. He was a key starter on two Super Bowl teams but he just never dominated the way you wanted him to, the way he's being paid to. And he played just 52 percent of the snaps in his nine games this year, which ranks 27th among starting interior linemen so far this year.

Great guy, natural leader, inspiring backstory, solid lineman. But hardly indispensable. Not when you also have Jalen Carter under contract and Moro Ojomo now in line for an offseason extension. The Eagles don't really have a third high-level rotational defensive tackle now – Ty Robinson, a 4th-round pick last year, will likely take over the role. But if you can get 1st- and 2nd-round draft picks for essentially a part-time player that's a no-brainer.

Add it up and Roseman got 1st-round picks in 2027 and 2028, 2nd-round picks in 2027, 2028 and 2029 and a couple 2027 5th-round picks to boot for a beat-up wide receiver, a fading interior lineman and a defensive tackle who hasn't lived up to expectations.

The way Roseman drafts, most of those picks are going to turn into important pieces as the Eagles build back toward respectability.

There hasn't been a whole lot to celebrate on the field this year, and everything points to more of the same over these last eight games.

But up on the second floor of the Jefferson Health Training Complex, Roseman is doing all he can to make sure it doesn't happen again.
