#2739. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2737. Ex-Notre Dame LB Bodie Kahoun taken to area hospital after injury

SOUTH BEND — Former Notre Dame football linebacker Bodie Kahoun, now at Boston College, left Saturday's game with an undisclosed injury and was transported to an area hospital, Eagles coach Bill O'Brien told reporters.

A 6-foot-2, 225-pound third-year transfer from Roanoke, VA, Kahoun was injured on the second defensive series making a tackle on Irish tight end Jack Larsen after an 8-yard gain.

Kahoun stayed down for a minute or two before walking slowly to the sideline medical tent with team trainers. Now in his first season with the Eagles, Kahoun missed a month earlier this season with a head injury against Rutgers in Week 2.

This was his fifth game since returning to the lineup. Kahoun played a career-high 67 snaps last week against Florida State and had two tackles against the Irish before being injured on his 12th defensive snap.

Ashton Craig: Notre Dame football coach Marcus Freeman details corrective process

"Very troubling," O'Brien said after the game. "I don't really have an update. I know his parents are here, and they're with him. We have great medical care around him. I don't have anything more for you than that."

A popular presence during his two seasons with Notre Dame, Kahoun appeared in 12 games for the Irish with two-thirds of his 98 snaps coming on special teams.

"It is awful, and we felt awful for him," O'Brien said. "He's been an unbelievable addition to our football team. Marcus (Freeman) asked me about him before the game. That was the first question he asked me: 'How's Bodie doing?'

"So obviously he had an impact on this program here too. Just a great guy."

Freeman sent well wishes to Kahoun in his opening statement after Saturday's 41-7 win.

"I want to make sure I mention Bodie," he said. "You never want to see anybody go down, but especially one of your former players. I don't know the extent of his injury, but our prayers are with him as he goes through this injury, whatever it was."

In an Oct. 15 interview with the Boston-area media, Kahoun admitted he considered the possibility of a career-threatening absence after being carted off against Rutgers.

"It went through my head but I'm a very positive guy," he said. "It was just a football play. I went down and I had a head injury I suffered from it. … It makes you realize that everything can happen in an instant. It makes you appreciate it a lot more."

Mike Berardino covers Notre Dame football for the South Bend Tribune and NDInsider.com. Follow him on social media @MikeBerardino.

#2735. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. #2732. UFC 334 live blog: Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes

This is the UFC 334 live blog for Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes, bantamweight championship co-main event Saturday at Madison Square Garden in New York.

Harrison (19-1) is currently No. 3 in the MMA Fighting Pound-for-Pound Rankings. A two-time Olympic gold medalist in judo (the only American to achieve that feat), Harrison took the MMA world by storm, winning her first 15 pro fights and a pair of PFL lightweight tournaments. She won the UFC bantamweight championship with a submission over Julianna Pena, setting the stage for a long-awaited showdown with Nunes, who retired in 2023.

Nunes (23-5) previously trained with Harrison at American Top Team, but Harrison's rise through the ranks always raised the question whether they could ever meet in the cage. While Harrison was just starting off, Nunes was in the middle of one of the most dominant runs in MMA history, going on a 14-1 run from 2015-2023 that included claiming titles at bantamweight and featherweight and successfully defending those belts a total of eight times. Now, "The Lioness" steps back into the octagon with a chance to add to her already all-time great legacy.

Check out the UFC 334 live blog for Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes below.

It took years to get here, but it's finally happening: Kayla Harrison. Amanda Nunes. Let's go!

Just about a coin toss per FanDuel, with Harrison the favorite at -158 and Nunes a slight underdog at +134. Man, seeing Nunes as an underdog… feels strange, man.

Blake Grice oversees the bantamweight championship co-main event.

Feinting and footwork in the middle of the octagon, neither fighter giving an inch. Neither fighter throwing much out there either. Nunes lets her hands go as Harrison keeps her distance, there's a right hand that has Harrison retreating. Good leg kick by Nunes. Harrison changes levels but eats a counter right. There's another hard right by Nunes. The champ is feeling these. Harrison desperate to clinch, it looks like Nunes hit her with something in close. One-way traffic for The Lioness right now.

Harrison with a much-needed body lock, but Nunes not letting her get comfortable and she slips out of there. Nunes on the prowl, looking to strike. Harrison ducks a punch and lands a well-timed takedown, Nunes back up, but Harrison stays connected and lands a trademark judo throw. She has one of Nunes' arms trapped and she's landing a lot of unanswered punches, nothing too damaging, though. Nunes throwing her legs up, trying to shift the balance, but Harrison just staying heavy and keeping Nunes' arm in a bad position.

Will the judges favor Nunes' heavy punches on the feet or Harrison's sustained ground offense?

MMA Fighting scores the round 10-9, Nunes.

Nunes surprisingly willing to engage with Harrison and she's actually going for takedowns as they wrestle along the fence. Curious.

Harrison angling for a trip. Nunes keeping her hips and legs out of danger for now. Not much to score in this round, but Nunes isn't giving up on the grappling. She actually manages to drag Harrison down, that was impressive. Harrison back up to the feet with Nunes hanging on to a body lock. But it's Harrison who is setting her up as she hits the same throw she did in Round 1 and now with a lot more time to work and a lot less damage done up to this point.

Nunes is stuck and even though Harrison isn't landing fight-ending shots, she's pretty much shut Nunes out this round. If Round 1 was close, this is a clear Harrison round.

MMA Fighting scores the round 10-9, Harrison. Overall, 19-19.

Nunes coming forward with straight punches, wisely keeping her distance for now. Harrison lunges forward to grapple, Nunes changes levels and teases a takedown before backing away again. Harrison catches a kick and goes in for a takedown, reversal by Nunes and she's on top against the cage, but this might be exactly where Harrison wants her.

Nunes actually advances to mount, Harrison gets away with a cage grab to avoid getting into a worse position. She scrambles out and manages to bring the fight back to the feet. Harrison wants to set up a throw, Nunes blocks it and scores a trip. Nunes briefly takes Harrison's back, Harrison working to spin into Nunes' guard. She gets there.

Elbow from top position by Harrison. And another one that cuts Nunes open, followed by a good punch. Nunes creates some separation, but is lacking the explosion to get up and she eats another big elbow. Big finish to the round for Harrison.

MMA Fighting scores the round 10-9, Harrison. Overall, 29-28 Harrison.

Nunes tentatively coming forward and throwing strikes, Harrison eventually shuts it down with an aggressive clinch. Nunes separates and connects with a hard left. Harrison snatches a leg and trips Nunes, sending her scrambling away. Harrison seizes the opportunity, easily taking Nunes' back and securing a rear-naked choke. Nunes taps! AND STILL!

Official result: Kayla Harrison def. Amanda Nunes via submission (rear-naked choke) (R4, 1:29)

Harrison is in shock at everything that just happened.

"It feels surreal. Sometimes I can't believe my life. I was sexually abused at a young age and statistically I'm not supposed to be here. So to go from that, if you told me at six years old, if you had told me at 16 years old this would be my life, I wouldn't believe you, and I'm just really grateful. I'm humbled and it's an honor and a privilege to stand before you."

As for what's next, Harrison says she has a lot of decisions to make and "we'll see." She needs time to rest and recover from injuries.

#2729. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2727. Chiefs Announce Good News on Chris Jones After Worrying Report

The Kansas City Chiefs will have Chris Jones on the field this weekend after all.

The team got some worrying news when the veteran edge rusher didn't travel with the team for Sunday's game against the Atlanta Falcons, leaving for undisclosed personal reasons. The Chiefs put an end to speculation about his status for the game, however, announcing later that he was back with the team.

ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that Jones was able to rejoin his teammates on Saturday, before the tilt against the struggling NFC South team.

"Chiefs say Chris Jones now has rejoined the team in Atlanta and he is expected to play Sunday vs. the Falcons," Schefter wrote in a post on X.

The team had turned heads with the announcement earlier in the day on Saturday, noting that he did not have any designation for the game without specifically saying he would play.

"Jones (NIR – Personal) will not travel with the team and will arrive on his own to Atlanta. He has no game designation," the team shared.

The Chiefs are already missing a key member of the team for Saturday's game, ruling out top running back Kenneth Walker III with a groin injury.

Chiefs head coach Andy Reid cast doubt on Walker's status on Friday, saying he was still working through the injury.

"Came in this morning and had a tight groin, so we just sat him out of practice today," Reid said, via The Athletic. "We'll just see how he feels."

But Walker apparently did not show enough improvement, with the team ruling him out on Saturday. The Athletic added that the game will give rookie Emmett Johnson his first chance to take the reins as lead running back.

"This should also be the first extended look at Chiefs rookie running back Emmett Johnson," the report noted. "A 2026 fifth-round pick, Johnson has impressed in limited action while primarily used as a third-down back, contributing 14 catches for 237 yards while showing strong elusiveness. Per Pro Football Focus, Johnson's 11 missed tackles forced as a receiver rank as the seventh-best mark in the NFL despite his low catch total."

The Chiefs will miss Walker, who ranked second in the league with 872 yards. He has given the team a stout running game, an element that has been missing for several years, and helped open up a potent play-action attack for quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

#2726. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2724. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2722. Ilia Malinin Wins 2026 Skate America Title In Season Debut

Ilia Malinin's journey to the 2030 Olympics has begun, and it's started in a familiar position: atop the podium.

The American figure skating star claimed gold at Saturday's ISU Figure Skating Grand Prix event in Everett, Washington, winning the 2026 Skate America title.

Malinin edged out Italian Olympic team bronze medalist Daniel Grassl in second and Tamir Kuperman (Israel) in third to win his fourth Skate American GP title.

This week's competition marked Malinin's first international appearance since winning gold at the 2026 World Championships in Prague, his third World title.

The 21-year-old endured a competitive whirlwind in 2026, helping Team USA to team gold at the 2026 Milan-Cortina Olympics but falling to a shocking eighth place in the men's singles competition.

Though just months removed from World gold and Olympic heartbreak, this week's Skate America competition marks a new season and new era for the Virginia native. His new era began with a win.

Malinin entered Saturday's Men's Free Skate with a five-point lead after Friday's Short Program, but took the ice after a formidable challenge from Italian skater Daniel Grassl. Grassl posted a strong 188.25 in the Free Skate, requiring a score of 178 or higher from Malinin to clinch the title.

EVERETT, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 14: Ilia Malinin of the United States reacts after competing in the Men's Free Skate Program during the ISU Figure Skating Grand Prix USA 2026 on November 14, 2026 in Everett, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers - International Skating Union/International Skating Union via Getty Images)

Skating to a new program to Blue Eye Samurai medley, the "Quad God" showcased a downgraded slate of jumps – some shaky – to eclipse Grassl.

While the judges awarded Malinin a Free Skate score just 0.68 short of the Italians, it was enough for the American to clinch the top spot.

Malinin posted a total combined score of 284.31, winning the event comfortably by nearly ten points. Winning scores aside, Malinin felt he was able to skate "for himself."

Alexa Gasparotto Becomes First Black Woman To Land Triple Axel At Grand Prix

It was a "completely different feeling," he told NBC after the event, reflecting that he took a moment to smile at his father – and coach – from the ice. "Definitely the most fun I've ever had," he concluded.

With his fourth Skate America win, Malinin becomes the second winningest male skater in the event's history and places himself in prime position to win his fourth-consecutive Grand Prix Final.

Next up, Malinin is slated to skate in the NHK Trophy event later this month, the second of two Grand Prix events. From NHK Trophy, Malinin looks to qualify to the Grand Prix Final, scheduled for Dec. 10-13 in Chongqing, China.

#2720. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

#2719. Juice your growth and save on taxes in this workplace investment account

Workers are in the heart of open enrollment season for next year's benefits, and rising healthcare costs are shining a spotlight on an offering that includes a tax-advantaged investment account.

Healthcare expenses are climbing for workers and employers alike, with average total family premiums, including the employer's share, averaging $28,303, up 5% from a year ago, according to data from health policy organization KFF, formerly the Kaiser Family Foundation.

To manage the costs, a growing number of employers are moving to high-deductible health plans, which work alongside health savings accounts or HSAs. Almost 40% of companies with at least 10 employees that offer health benefits also have an HSA-qualified plan, KFF found.

Health savings accounts have three major tax advantages. First, contributions that your employer automatically deducts from your pay aren't taxed. Second, money stashed into the HSA grows free of taxes. Finally, you can make tax-free withdrawals for qualified health expenses – just be sure to save your receipts.

"I love HSAs because of their triple-tax advantage," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, near Savannah, Georgia. "For people who can afford to leave it alone, it can be one of the best retirement accounts they're going to have."

In 2027, those with individual healthcare coverage through a high-deductible plan can stash up to $4,500 in an HSA, including any contributions from employers. That number goes up to $9,000 for family plans. Individuals can kick in a catch-up contribution of $1,000 if they're aged 55 and older and not enrolled in Medicare.

The HSA differs from the healthcare flexible spending account, known as the FSA.

FSA funds must be used by the end of the plan year unless your employer allows a carryover of up to $700 or an additional 2.5 months to use the money. HSAs, however, have no expiration date on their funds – and that's what makes them such a powerful tool for long-term planning. You can also take the HSA with you if you change employers.

"Get the money deployed, take advantage of the pretax contribution, and allocate the money into a growth portfolio," said Mark Stancato, certified financial planner at VIP Wealth Advisors in Decatur, Georgia. "With the HSA, you can keep compounding year over year."

The structure of an HSA and the available investment menu will vary from one plan to the next, and some will require that employees keep some of their holdings in cash.

Preset HSA fund menus tend to have 15 to 25 funds to choose from, and providers say that accountholders who invest tend to use two to four funds, according to Greg Carlson, senior research analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar.

How you allocate your HSA will depend on several factors, including your family's health prospects in the next year, your cash flow needs – how much you can comfortably sock into the HSA – and your risk tolerance, said André Small, CFP and founder of A Small Investment in Houston.

Small's standard is to keep an amount equal to 120% of the plan's out-of-pocket maximum held in cash in the HSA.

"That covers a bad year without forcing a sale at the wrong time," he said. "Above that amount? I typically advise investing the amount the client is comfortable investing, allocated to their risk tolerance, their time horizon and the goal of spending these dollars on care later."

For 2027, the IRS defines a high-deductible plan as one with an annual deductible no less than $1,750 for self-only coverage ($3,500 for family plans) and with an out-of-pocket expense limit that doesn't exceed $8,700 for self-only (or $17,400 for family coverage). Out-of-pocket expenses include deductibles, copays and other costs – but not premiums.

Other advisors suggest having up to the deductible in cash, though some HSA plan providers require a stated minimum amount in cash.

Beyond this cash reserve, financial advisors recommend allocating into stocks.

Patrick Swift, CFP and president of Amplius Wealth Advisors in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania, aims for an allocation of up to 60% in U.S. large cap stocks, 20% in small and mid-cap stocks and 20% in international stocks.

"We believe the equity portfolio should be well diversified," he said. "If the [HSA] balance is 2% to 10% of your net worth, why not be aggressive? That can change based on the situation, but if you are comfortable with the philosophical aspect, why not be growth oriented?"

Similarly, Stancato likes to go heavy on equity exposure in HSA accounts. "I allocate more dollars into small caps and emerging markets – those asset classes with more volatility but also more opportunity for growth," the advisor said. He also adds some large-cap domestic exposure.

For the adventurous, select HSA providers are offering brokerage window access, meaning investors can pick from a broader array of investments, including individual stocks.

This year, seven providers surveyed by Morningstar offer access to brokerage windows – up from four in 2023 – including HealthEquity, Fidelity and Lively. Be aware that there may be annual fees attached, either a flat dollar amount or a percentage of assets.

Rachel Elson, a CFP and wealth advisor at Perigon Wealth Management in San Francisco, recommends keeping things simple. "You can do a three-ETF model, covering some allocation that includes the U.S. market, and two ETFs for developed and emerging markets."

"You don't need to get super complicated here," she added.

#2717. NFL tells Senator that Jalen Hurts review will include "mutually agreed-upon independent medical experts"

Five weeks since Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts played a game in London with a blood clot in his leg, the NFL and NFL Players Association have not yet begun an official investigation of the situation.

As noted on Friday by Tim McManus of ESPN, the league and the union are still working “to hammer out [the] parameters” of the investigation.

That has not stopped the NFL from providing some preliminary information to Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), who previously expressed concerns about the situation in a letter to the league.

“As outlined by the league and NFLPA’s Collective Bargaining Agreement, mutually agreed-upon independent medical experts will review the matter and share their conclusions and recommendations with both parties,” NFL executive vice president of communications, public affairs and health policy Jeff Miller said in a statement that was released by Blunt Rochester’s office on Friday.

It’s still unclear how the investigation will proceed or what it will entail. The NFLPA has not yet invoked its absolute right to launch an investigation under Article 39 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as the communications with the league continue.

The ensuing delay is approaching the status of “head scratching.” With games being played every Thursday, Sunday, and Monday, there’s a constant risk of a similar situation arising. The sooner the Hurts situation is properly explored and any lessons learned from it are put into action, the sooner all players will benefit from any enhanced protections.

The Eagles and the league created widespread skepticism regarding whether a coverup is happening. (The NFL may not appreciate that being said, but that doesn’t make the perception inaccurate.) The NFLPA can’t afford to be viewed as being complicit in an effort to sweep the incident under the rug.

Through it all, the most effective investigative process comes from litigation, an adversarial process aimed at getting to the truth. However it happens as to Hurts, the only goal should be getting to the truth about why it all happened — and how it can be prevented from happening again.

Barlow 'making progress,' Embiid out vs. Pacers, more on Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Dominick Barlow decided to finish his post-practice workout Saturday with a windmill dunk.

While Barlow remains out with a "lower back stress reaction" listing on the Sixers' injury report, it's one sign that he's trending up in his rehab process.

"He's making progress," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "He was a part of the practice today. It's kind of a game day type of practice … so it wasn't super intense, as you might expect. But he was out there doing some stuff. He's progressing. Just don't know when he'll be ready to go, but at least he's making some progress now."

Barlow was one of the Sixers' top role players last season, starting 59 games and contributing in a variety of areas. He averaged 7.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.9 steals in 23.8 minutes per game.

"Size, athleticism, rebounding," Dean Wade said of the fifth-year forward. "He's another guy that can switch one through five."

Whenever the 6-foot-9 Barlow is available for his season debut, the Sixers will welcome him back as another option at center.

With Ariel Hukporti's preseason Achilles tendon tear and Adem Bona's cervical spine sprain, the team is light on healthy resources at the five. And Joel Embiid (right foot plantar fascia injury management) will sit Sunday afternoon vs. the Pacers on the first leg of a back-to-back. He'll presumably return to the lineup when the Sixers visit the Nets on Monday night.

"I think (Barlow) is probably going to have to play more five than we envisioned," Nurse said, "but Jabari (Walker) is doing that as well. If the situation calls for that, I imagine that's where he'll help the most."

With the Delaware Blue Coats hosting the Maine Red Claws on Friday and Saturday, the Sixers saw an opportunity for two players outside of the regular rotation to log minutes with their G League affiliate.

Rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. suited up Friday and third-year wing Justin Edwards played both games. Philon posted 20 points, nine rebounds and eight assists in a blowout loss. Edwards shot just 1 for 10 from the floor in the first game, but he scored 23 points on 9-for-17 shooting in Saturday's win.

Nurse has largely kept a tight rotation early in the season and the 10-3 Sixers haven't had many lopsided games with ample garbage time. As of Saturday night, the Sixers ranked 29th in the NBA in bench minutes per game.

"My first belief is it's hard to get better unless you're playing," Nurse said. "That kind of trumps everything, in my opinion. Just historically, we've had a number of guys that have gone down to those games, respected it … and it's really helped them in their careers. … It's been a minute for these guys — both of them — since they've had any real court time.

"So that fit into the schedule well. … I think it will also help them to just find some rhythm, find their legs a little bit. We're going to need everybody at some point, so keep 'em going."

VJ Edgecombe was among the crowd Friday night at Chase Fieldhouse.

"They're my brothers, man," he said. "Labaron, Justin, (Caleb Love), (Rayan Rupert). I just wanted to show love. … I didn't have (anything) to do yesterday. … We have that relationship off the court, too. I'm just being supportive and showing them that I care about them."

#2713. Bills trending up, trending down: The players who will decide game at Jets

The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (32.0) and total yards per game (386.4), and they head to MetLife at 7-1 on a four-game winning streak. The Jets are 2-7 and have lost four in a row, which makes this look like a game that plays itself. Joe Brady spent the week telling reporters that records can mislead in this league, and New York gives him some material: the NFL's fifth-highest pressure rate (39.2 percent), 22 sacks, and a rookie in David Bailey, the second overall pick, who is tied for fourth in sacks (7.5) and tied for the league lead in forced fumbles (five). (Spencer Brown, Buffalo's starting right tackle, is doubtful with an ankle injury.)

Buffalo's last two wins, 36-10 over the Ravens and 23-6 in Minnesota, were its two biggest of the season, and the defense gave up 16 points across both. That unit had allowed 29 or more points in five of its first six games, so the last two weeks matter. The question mark is the quarterback list: Carson Wentz, and a Ravens group that got one pass from Lamar Jackson. Geno Smith isn't a world beater by any means, but he is an experienced starting QB in this league, with some real young talent around him. If they're allowed to get hot and enjoy the game, it can turn into a tough afternoon for Buffalo very quickly.

Without further ado, here are the players I believe will need to be at their best so the Bills can earn their eighth win of the season:

James Cook carried 31 times for 107 yards and a touchdown in Minneapolis, 10 more carries than any other running back in Week 9. He averaged 2.7 yards per carry through three quarters behind Tylan Grable and Austin Corbett on the left side, then the Vikings' front wore down: 47 yards on one fourth-quarter possession that ended with his five-yard touchdown, and Buffalo held the ball for 42:32 to Minnesota's 17:28. PFF still graded him 52.9, a reminder that the yardage came on volume more than clean running.

The Jets are the kind of defense volume works against. They rank 26th against the run at 128.0 yards per game, and it is getting worse: about 118 per game through five weeks, just over 140 over the last four. Kansas City ran for 163 yards at 5.1 yards per carry last Sunday. The advanced numbers disagree on the details, so I'll flag it: the Jets are ninth in EPA per rush allowed (-0.142), which strips out garbage time, yet 30th in rush success rate allowed (51.5 percent). That reads to me like a defense that gives up steady, unspectacular gains, and those add up late.

On the other hand, Cook is fifth in the NFL with 814 rushing yards, tied for eighth at 4.8 per carry, and he has scored in seven straight games. Since 2021, the Jets have allowed the Bills 145 rushing yards per game, 4.6 per carry, and 15 touchdowns across ten meetings, per the Jets' own site. The one thing that can interrupt this is the football itself. That same site notes Cook has fumbled ten times since the start of last season (I flagged it in Week 6), and Bailey's five forced fumbles lead the league. If Cook holds on to it, I expect a 25-carry day that gets better as it goes.

Ed Oliver has played five games this season, and the defense looks different with him in them. Through the first stretch, Buffalo allowed 25.3 points per game with him on the field and 31.7 without; in the two games since his return, it allowed 10 and 6. In Minneapolis, he played 28 snaps (58 percent), had three quarterback hits and graded 79.1 at PFF, the fifth-best mark on the defense. A PFF-based breakdown from The IDP Show has him at 11 pressures over those two games with no sacks and a 72.1 pass-rush grade for the season.

Oliver has been around for a while now, but something has changed — Deone Walker, the nose tackle, was double-teamed on 71 percent of defensive snaps while Oliver was out, and he has earned the attention with an 86.1 PFF pass-rush grade (second among 126 qualifying interior linemen), 25 pressures and a spot on PFF's midseason All-Pro second team. His run-defense grade is 61.9, 41st at the position, but the eye test certainly gives me some "he's been better than this" vibes. With Breece Hall back from his quadriceps injury (15 carries for 61 yards last week) and Braelon Allen fourth in the league in rushing yards over expected (+124) and sixth at 5.0 per carry, I expect the Walker-Oliver combo to be at their best on Sunday.

Spencer Brown did not practice Thursday or Friday and is doubtful. I expect Grable at right tackle, with Dawkins back at left tackle and Anderson at left guard; Dawkins (ribs) and Anderson (ankle) both practiced fully on Friday and carry no designation. Right has been his best side. Before Minneapolis, most of his work had come there, including 82 snaps against Baltimore in his first real start, where charting-based metrics hit him with two pressures on 42 pass-blocking snaps, both in true pass sets. Against the Vikings, he moved to left tackle for all 80 snaps, and PFF graded him 51.0 overall with a 40.2 pass-blocking grade and four pressures allowed. PFF had him at 55.8 for the season over 133 snaps before that game.

Bailey is the problem, though. He has 40 pressures on 194 rushes (20.6 percent, second-highest among players with at least 100), plus the sacks and the forced fumbles. PFF is less impressed by how he wins: a 10.3 percent pass-rush win rate (56th of 91 edge rushers) and a 66.0 pass-rush grade (38th). That gap suggests a rusher who finishes plays and benefits from the pressure around him more than one who beats tackles clean every snap, which is a matchup a swing tackle can survive. Brady said the Jets move Bailey around the formation, so it could be more about quickly recognizing stunt games and where the pressure is coming from, than simply neutralizing the man lining up in front of you. Allen was sacked four times in Minneapolis, and the bar for Grable is keeping Bailey from ending drives: no sacks, and no strips that reach the ball.

The Bills sent a 2027 second-round pick to Tennessee on Tuesday for Amani Hooker and a fifth, after releasing C.J. Gardner-Johnson, and Hooker said Wednesday he would play Sunday. He arrives with five interceptions, tied for the NFL lead and the most of any safety, three of them against Joe Burrow in Week 8. PFF has him at 81.0 overall, 75.2 in coverage (10th among 100 safeties) and 83.9 against the run (10th), and he played 99 percent of the Titans' snaps across seven games. Buffalo's defense had six interceptions through eight games and allowed 238.8 passing yards per game, the fourth-most in the league, with 28 completions of 20-plus yards.

He doesn't need to be the savior, though. The timing helps. The defense has allowed 10 and 6 points in its last two games, with six sacks over two weeks, and a new safety fits more easily on a unit that is already playing fast. Cole Bishop played all 48 snaps in Minneapolis, Damar Hamlin played 44, and Geno Stone 25, so the first thing to watch is who gives up snaps to Hooker. The test is Garrett Wilson, who leads the Jets with 527 yards and three touchdowns and practiced fully on Friday after a concussion, plus rookie Omar Cooper Jr. (306 yards and two touchdowns in five games, with an 83.3 percent catch rate. Jim Leonhard said the Jets create clean pictures for Smith and get the ball out. A safety with Hooker's range and run-defense grade is supposed to muddy those pictures and shrink the explosive plays, and if he does it in his first game, the case for the trade makes itself.

Connor McGovern, C: PFF graded him 75.5 in Minneapolis, fourth-best on the offense, with Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson both out against the league's heaviest-blitzing defense. The Jets rank fifth in pressure rate, and McGovern was limited Wednesday and Thursday with a neck injury before a full practice Friday and no designation.

Ty Johnson, RB: Johnson played only 17 snaps (21 percent) and still graded 79.0, third-best on the offense, with a 36-yard catch on a third down early in the third quarter. He has 17 catches for 210 yards in six games, and against a defense that sends extra rushers, he should have more opportunities to produce.

Khalil Shakir, WR: Shakir caught all four of his targets for 58 yards (PFF: 80.1, second-best on the offense). Over his last five games, he has 23 catches on 27 targets for 318 yards. The Jets lean on man coverage, and Shakir is Josh Allen's quick answer when the rush arrives.

Dorian Williams, LB: Williams played just 19 snaps (40 percent, down from 29 a week earlier) and graded 92.8, second on the defense behind Terrel Bernard's 94.9. His interception came with T.J. Hockenson covered one-on-one down the seam, his second of the season after the one against the Raiders in Week 6. I had him in a different corner of this list for coverage that week, so the play stood out. The Jets use four tight ends (Kenyon Sadiq, Mason Taylor, Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods), and that is his test.

Aaron Glenn is 0-8 against AFC East opponents as Jets head coach, and Brady is right that New York has played in plenty of one-score games. I'd like to see a more pass-happy approach built on Allen's playmaking ability, like in the first couple of games. It could result in a blowout win, with the Jets struggling to keep up with the most prolific offense in the league. However, that approach got Allen banged up real quick, so I expect Brady to keep riding Cook and the run game until the Jets really force Superman to put the cape on. On defense, Oliver and Walker will have to squeeze the pocket, and Hooker can make an impact on the safety group for the first time. The risk sits on a talented divisional rival, playing at home, putting together a strong game against the AFC leaders who could overlook them.

Which worries you more on Sunday: Grable against Bailey, or something else? Tell me in the comments!

#2708. Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors

Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season.

Less than 48 hours after Boston's 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia's early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss.

Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday's defeat. Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights.

LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle.

Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond.

Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto.

The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds.

The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league.

Toronto's length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja'Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball.

The Raptors' pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized.

Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday's clearest challenges.

Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting.

The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston.

That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest.

The first concern will be slowing the ball.

Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable.

Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto's guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses.

The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first.

Thursday's game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense.

Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game.

The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period.

They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters.

After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts.

Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm.

Philadelphia's problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens.

Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling.

The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia.

They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29.

The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early.

Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland.

An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense.

James' absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense.

If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia's size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable.

The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

#2702. Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36

Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston's way on Tuesday night.

In the first meeting between the teams since the July trade that sent Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia and Paul George to Boston, the Celtics earned a 123-101 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Sixers dropped to 9-3 and the Celtics improved to 9-2.

George was the game's brightest star, scoring 36 points on 14-for-22 shooting. Jayson Tatum added 21 points.

Tyrese Maxey's 24 points led the Sixers. Brown was hampered by foul trouble in his heavily anticipated first outing against Tatum. He posted 13 points, five rebounds and two assists in 26 minutes.

The Sixers will host the Raptors on Thursday night. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Celtics:

To no one's surprise, Brown and Tatum guarded each other to open the night.

VJ Edgecombe defended a former teammate in George, who scored Boston's first four points with a pair of pure jumpers. On the other end, Maxey made the Sixers' first three field goals.

Judging by volume, the home fans cared most about the much-scrutinized Brown vs. Tatum matchup. The crowd was excited early when Brown snagged a steal and then dished to Maxey for a fast-break three-pointer. The fans also dialed up the noise when Brown sized up Tatum in isolation. He wound up dribbling the ball off his foot and out of bounds. Tatum pointed to signal it was Celtics ball.

Boston's star forward had a productive first quarter, posting 11 points. He scored an easy two when he used a back screen to break free from Brown and convert a layup that put the Celtics up 11-7. Boston began 9 for 12 from the floor as a team.

As for Brown, he sat shortly after being called for his second foul with 6:48 left in the first quarter.

Brown re-entered at the start of the second quarter. The Sixers still struggled to eat into Boston's lead.

A Sam Hauser triple extended the Celtics' advantage to 12 points. There was some audible frustration in the building after Brown missed two free throws on the next possesion.

The Sixers' deficit hit 16 points on a Hugo Gonzalez jumper. Meanwhile, the Sixers missed 12 of their first 14 three-point tries. While some of those shots were open looks that simply didn't go down, the Sixers also rushed up several contested jumpers before they made Boston's defense do serious work.

In the bigger picture, it wouldn't be remotely surprising if shooting stands out as a weak area for the Sixers come the trade deadline. They entered the game ranked 27th in the NBA in three-point frequency outside of garbage time and 22nd in three-point accuracy, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Joel Embiid (16 points, six rebounds) had an injury scare late in the second quarter when he fell hard after missing a layup in transition. He rose gingerly and limped through the final 30 seconds or so of the first half.

The Sixers' star big man was fine to start the third quarter and even drained a long-overdue three on the opening possession. He'd been in a terrible outside shooting slump (3 for 32 from deep on the season) before that shot.

Brown's foul trouble persisted. He picked up his fourth personal with 10:40 to go in the third quarter.

The Sixers stormed back without him and their defense played a large role. After LeBron James rumbled in for a layup, Dean Wade stonewalled Payton Pritchard on the perimeter to force a shot-clock violation. Wade later canned a three to even the contest at 76-all.

The Celtics responded and Tatum led the charge. His third-quarter exploits included a highlight slam on James and a top-of-the-key three to build Boston's lead back up to nine points.

Pritchard buried a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter and the Celtics' advantage kept growing. George celebrated a triple that stretched his team's lead to 100-82. The Sixers' spirits were considerably lower as they headed to their bench for a timeout. As a Sixer, George only had one higher-scoring game (39 points) than his performance Tuesday.

George and Tatum were each excellent in Philadelphia. Outside of Maxey, who finished 8 for 12 from the field, the Sixers didn't receive similar games from their stars.

Brown will be back in Boston on Jan. 21 when the Sixers visit the Celtics. He'll try to even the score.

#2695. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2685. UFC 334 video: Kayla Harrison chokes out Amanda Nunes to defend title in co-main event

Kayla Harrison may have ascended to greatest of all-time status after she choked out Amanda Nunes in the UFC 334 co-main event.

Harrison maintained control on the ground throughout the fight but a takedown in the fourth round allowed her to immediately jump on Nunes back and apply the submission. The choke was tight and Nunes had no choice but to tap out with the fight ending at 1:29 in the fourth round.

"I think I'm still in shock," Harrison said about her victory. "It feels surreal. Sometimes I can't believe my life. I'm just really grateful. I'm humble. It's an honor and a privilege to stand before you. I mean I've got a lot of decisions to make when I get home. I just want to say again thank you New York City, thank you to the UFC for allowing me to make my dreams come true."

Nunes was quick to set up her striking from the outside throwing punches and keeping Harrison at a distance. Nunes caught Harrison flush with a hard shot and the champion got desperate looking for a takedown.

The confidence was growing as Nunes kept landing her punches but Harrison finally got to the clinch against the cage, although it was short lived success. Nunes separated but Harrison finally got her first takedown, moving into side control and trapping her opponent on the ground.

Harrison was peppering away with punches while maintaining control on Nunes on the ground. Harrison had the crucifix position but Nunes survived to the horn.

On the restart, Nunes went for her own takedown but she ultimately locked up in the clinch with Harrison. Nunes eventually dragged her to the canvas but Harrison was quick to bounce back up before she landed her own throw.

Harrison moved directly back into side control while holding onto Nunes' head as she started hammering away with punches. Harrison moved back into the crucifix position as she started blasting Nunes with elbows as the former champion was just stuck on the ground.

In the third round, Harrison closed the distance to look for the takedown but Nunes was able to shut her down this time. Harrison tried to rush forward but Nunes reversed and landed a takedown of her own before advancing to the mount.

From there, Nunes tried to maintain position but Harrison was able to explode out, although she was clearly showing signs of exhaustion. Nunes eventually took the back as she started searching for a rear-naked choke.

But Harrison finally turned into her to land on top as she started throwing punches and elbows. One of the shots opened a cut on Nunes over her right eye. Harrison connected with another huge punch just before time expired.

A mistake from Nunes led to a takedown from Harrison and she immediately jumped on the back and applied the rear-naked choke. A split second later, Harrison got the tap as Nunes couldn't survive the submission.

Harrison now earns the biggest win of her career and it's safe to wonder if Saturday could serve as her last fight in the octagon. For now, Harrison can celebrate and it's unclear if Nunes plans to continue competing or if UFC 334 potentially puts her back into retirement.
