#2682. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."

#2677. Jokic, Murray help Nuggets hand Pelicans a sixth straight loss

NEW ORLEANS (AP) — Nikola Jokic had 26 points, eight rebounds and 10 assists, Jamal Murray added 23 points, seven rebounds and nine assists, and the Denver Nuggets outlasted the New Orleans Pelicans 116-108 on Saturday night.

Denver has won four of its last five games and moved to 3-0 against the Pelicans this season. New Orleans dropped its sixth consecutive contest, four of which have come at home.

Jokic was on triple-double watch, shooting 9 of 14 from the field. Murray shot 9 of 16 and was a team-high +16.

Zion Williamson led New Orleans with 24 points. Saddiq Bey added 16 points, and rookie guard Jaron Pierre Jr. scored 13 in 23 minutes after scoring 23 points for the G-League Laketown Squadron's inaugural home game earlier Saturday afternoon.

CLEVELAND (AP) — Tyrese Proctor posted his first triple-double with 24 points, 11 rebounds and a career-best 10 assists in leading short-handed Cleveland to a victory over Dallas.

Australia native Proctor became the first Cleveland player with a triple-double since Max Strus against Charlotte on April 14, 2024. The points and assists were new career-highs for Proctor, and he also matched his pro high in rebounds.

The Cavaliers played without their entire usual starting lineup as Donovan Mitchell (left knee), James Harden (left calf), Evan Mobley (left big toe), Jarrett Allen (right knee) and Peyton Watson (right hamstring) were sidelined with injuries. Sixth man Sam Merrill (right hamstring) also was inactive. The Cavs ruled out all of their starters after travel delays following the nationwide ground stop on Friday and having to stay overnight in South Florida after a loss to the Miami Heat.

Former Cleveland guard Kyrie Irving scored 20 of his 34 points in the third quarter for Dallas, while Cooper Flagg had 18 points and eight rebounds. Flagg hugged fellow 2025 draftee — and former college teammate — Proctor shortly after he earned his 10th assist on a pass to Mario Hezonja.

MEMPHIS, Tenn. (AP) — Cedric Coward had 23 points and 12 rebounds and Taylor Hendricks scored a career-high 22 as Memphis built an early lead and defeated Brooklyn.

A night after a 142-111 victory over New Orleans featured 10 Memphis players reaching double figures, tying an NBA record, seven Grizzlies reached double figures against the Nets. Javon Small scored 19 and Cam Spencer finished with 17 and eight assists as Memphis won its third in the last four.

Julius Randle lead Brooklyn with 22 points and Day'Ron Sharpe added 16 points and 11 rebounds as Brooklyn lost its third in the last four. Noah Clowney scored 15.

Memphis built a 20-point first-half lead behind 3-point success and weathered a third quarter Brooklyn burst that cut the advantage to single digits. By early in the fourth quarter, Memphis had taken the lead back to 24.

MIAMI (AP) — Giannis Antetokounmpo had 34 points, 14 rebounds and eight assists, some of the spectacular variety, and the Miami Heat beat the Detroit Pistons 137-117 on Saturday night for their fourth straight win.

Klay Thompson scored 26 points in his return from a sprained ankle and Bam Adebayo added 20 for the Heat. Davion Mitchell had 15 points and nine rebounds for Miami.

Cade Cunningham had 33 points and eight assists for Detroit, which got 20 points and seven assists from Kevin Huerter.

Miami had nine players record at least one block and finished with 14 as a team — one shy of the franchise record.

The NBA record for players on the same team having at least one block in a game is 10, done twice — both by Golden State, first in 1991 and then again in 2016. The Heat team record for players with at least one block was eight, done on five occasions.

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Norman Powell scored 23 points, Matas Buzelis added 18 points and nine rebounds, and short-handed Chicago won for the second night in a row with a victory over Minnesota..

Buddy Hield and Tre Jones each chipped in 16 points off the bench for the Bulls, who ended Minnesota's five-game winning streak convincingly.

Chicago's travel to Minneapolis on Friday was delayed by the nationwide ground stop that impacted many flights across the country. That meant the Bulls didn't arrive to Minnesota until the day of the game Saturday after beating the Hawks in Chicago on Friday.

The travel disruption didn't seem to impact the Bulls, nor did a limited roster. Rookie Caleb Wilson is out for an extended period with a fractured hand. Jalen Smith also missed Saturday's game with a hand injury, and center Nic Claxton was sidelined with a hamstring injury.

Buzelis picked up the scoring in their absence with 14 first-half points.

The Timberwolves missed their first 13 shots from 3-point range and finished 9 for 38.

Minnesota was held to 17 points in the first quarter, its lowest-scoring quarter of the season. The Wolves failed to reach 110 points for the first time this season.

#2674. Don Willard to serve as the head referee for 2 NFL games on same day after league switches up assignments

NFL referee Don Willard is set to serve as the head referee for two NFL games in the same day. It is not readily known whether this has happened before, according to The Athletic.

He's being pressed into double duty because of the league scrambling to reassign officiating crews due to travel issues caused by Friday's unprecedented four-hour nationwide ground stop for domestic flights in the United States.

This impacted travel plans across sports leagues, including a college football game between Ole Miss and Oklahoma, which was moved to Sunday.

It didn't impact start times for any NFL games, but it did force the league to switch up some referee assignments.

Willard and his crew — umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew — will begin the day calling the Miami Dolphins-Indianapolis Colts game, set to kick off at 1 p.m. ET in Indiana.

After the game, Willard and Co. will then drive 110 miles to Cincinnati, Ohio, to call the Pittsburgh Steelers-Cincinnati Bengals game for Week 10's "Sunday Night Football," which begins at 8:20 p.m. ET.

While only three officiating crew changes were needed, one could be for the history books.

Willard has been an NFL official for nine years, including officiating six playoff games. He typically serves as a side judge for Scott Novak's crew.

The NFL made the reassignments based on driving distance from officials' hometowns. The other two moves were to have umpire Barry Anderson take over for Alex Moore in the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Tennessee Titans, while Duane Heydt steps in for Shawn Smith in the Carolina Panthers-New Orleans Saints NFC South battle.

Originally, Carl Cheffers was supposed to referee the Miami-Indianapolis game, while Clete Blakeman was supposed to lead the Pittsburgh-Cincinnati game.

Willard will now be the head referee for both games.

#2673. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

#2668. Steelers' soft zone scheme could have big problems with Bengals QB Joe Burrow

The Pittsburgh Steelers will travel to face the Cincinnati Bengals in an NFL Week 10 rematch that has major implications for the AFC North race.

The former prevailed by a 30-27 margin when these teams first faced off in September in a back-and-forth affair that ended with the Pittsburgh defense stopping a late bid by quarterback Joe Burrow and the Bengals offense to tie the game or take the lead late.

The winner will take a one-game lead in the division. If the Steelers win, they'll own the head-to-head tiebreaker at the end of the season. If the Bengals win, they'll enjoy a favorable schedule to stay one step ahead of first-year coach Mike McCarthy's team.

Here's USA TODAY's guide on what to look for in the matchup, which will air nationally on NBC's "Sunday Night Football."

Required reading: 3 questions that will make or break the second half of the Steelers season

The Bengals star came as close as anyone has all season to solving Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Patrick Graham's revamped system designed to avoid getting beat on long pass plays.

Burrow completed 28 of 37 passes for 282 yards and three touchdowns during the initial Week 3 matchup. He found four different receivers for gains of at least 20 yards, and two of his three scoring tosses came from outside the red zone.

The Steelers have done a nice job of keeping the play in front of them since, a major reason they're allowing just 14.25 points per game during their current four-game winning streak.

Burrow has the receiving talent to challenge that success once again. Ja'Marr Chase has 647 yards and seven touchdowns already in 2026. Counterpart Tee Higgins has been even better with 758 yards and six scores.

It should be quite the battle of wits, with Burrow likely holding the advantage as he gets the start at home at Paycor Stadium.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

As good as Burrow was against Pittsburgh in that first meeting, the Steelers quarterback was even more efficient. He averaged 8.6 yards per attempt in piling up a total of 292 and three touchdowns, plus a tipped interception.

The big plays came early and often. Running back Jaylen Warren took the first pass of the game for a 30-yard gain en route to piling up 176 yards from scrimmage.

Tight end Darnell Washington had a 47-yard catch. Receiver Roman Wilson added a 38-yard touchdown. Tight end Pat Freiermuth and receiver Ben Skowronek added receptions of at least 20 yards of their own.

It was a sharp contrast to what we've seen from McCarthy's offense since. Amid injuries to Wilson and fellow receiver Michael Pittman Jr., the playcalling has learned into the running game with Warren and a short-and-quick passing attack that's decent at moving the chains but not so great at piling up yardage in bunches.

It will therefore be interesting to see to what degree McCarthy tries to stick with what worked against the Bengals versus what's worked against the rest of the schedule so far.

The Steelers defense has smothered opposing running games. It's allowing an average of just 55 yards on the ground over the past four games.

The Bengals running back, however, has been kryptonite for the group over his past four outings against Pittsburgh.

He's averaged 6.25 yards per carry and totaled 338 yards over the span, which has forced the Steelers to respect the run while seeking principally to slow Burrow, Chase and Higgins.

Pittsburgh has benefitted from being able to make opposing offenses one dimensional, so keep an eye on the amount of balance Brown is able to give Cincinnati in this one.

#2660. What we learned from the Spurs win over the Warriors

I was about 12 years old when I realized that there were people in the Dark Ages who had lived amongst the ruins of the Roman Empire.

Once a week in my art class (usually on a Friday) we were given free reign to pursue whatever we wanted, so long as it pertained to either the creation or study of art.

Being a poor visual artist, I tended to opt for study, and would plop myself into a beanbag chair in the corner of the room with a stack of art books.

In the time before the proliferation of google image searches this felt like a revelation, and I spent countless hours pouring through volumes of paintings that I'd otherwise only have seen in a museum.

I can still recall the goosebumpy thrill of stumbling into the deeply shadowed chiaroscuro of El Greco, or the eerie moonlit majesty of John Atkinson Grimshaw.

But it was a piece by the French Romantic painter Hubert Robert, found in a compendium of work contained in the Philadelphia Museum of Art, that so confounded me that I begged my teacher to make me a photocopy of it.

I kept my humble paper copy of 'Ruins of a Roman Bath with Washerwomen' in a manila folder on my childhood bookshelf for many years.

From time to time I would take it out and just stare at it. I couldn't understand why it had captured me so, but I knew it had something to do with the nature of the situation.

If you've seen it, you know that it depicts a towering Roman edifice surrounding a once-ornate bathhouse. It's clear that the architecture is no longer being maintained. The age is visible. There are stones missing.

And yet, it's still so majestic. The ruin itself testifies to the grandeur that came before.

The structure is still enormous and strong, and I suspect that one of the first thoughts that anyone has looking at it, is to wonder what it must have looked like at the peak of the empire.

If it were just a painting of those ruins, it would be arresting enough as is.

Gathered around the edges of the previously opulent pool, are hunched over figures, doing their laundry in the remains of the bathhouse.

I had developed quite a real fondness for the subject of history by the age of twelve, but this was something that had never occurred to me.

People had continued living in Roman ruins.

I suppose some part of my brain had to have registered this, knowing that the Colosseum was still standing, but to me, ruins weren't a place where people lived.

Sure, if they were important enough, maybe someone would build a museum, and people would come to visit them, but the thought of anyone actually living there was astonishing.

But people had in fact done that. It's all over the historical record. They did their best to maintain the plumbing and the roads, and the structures, and just stayed where they were.

Crusaders patched and fortified them. Some people carried on as if the Western Empire still existed, awiating a return to glory that never came.

Last night I felt that familiar feeling washing over me any time I saw Warriors fans in the crowd, as the Spurs punctured any illusions of a lingering Golden State greatness.

It's one thing to witness the fall of an empire. It's another thing altogether to keep living there.

For a moment (and in spite of Draymond Green's flagrant antics), I felt a wave of pity wash over me. It quickly turned to empathy with the realization that I too had been there.

Thirty points down at the half, with an all-too-clear vision of the future in front of them, these people were still holding on to a return to glory. Maybe not in this game, but to the season as a whole.

Steph Curry turns 39 in March. Draymond Green hasn't been an offensive plus in years. Jimmy Butler is still to return from an ACL injury at an age where recovery is negligible.

Promising rookie Yaxel Lendeborg was learning hard lessons about facing the defense of true contenders (he went 1-13), and probably won't be up to speed in the way that aging squad needs as they approach their 40's.

There's no young Kawhi Leonard to tie everything together. The sun is setting. Has, realistically, already set.

There are still people doing their laundry in the ruins.

And who am I to blame them? If not for the arrival of a certain French sensation, I'd probably be right there with them.

But it does speak to the difference in approaches from the two franchises.

Pursuing longevity, the Popovich/Duncan-era Spurs almost never cashed in all their chips for an all-or-nothing swing at a title. They kept building as they went. And when the end of their run was well and truly visible, they looked at what they had left and tried to repurpose it in a productive way.

It's not terribly dissimilar from what some of those old Roman communities did.

Recognizing the end for what it was, the citizens of cities like Avneches, Aosta, and Split began to build their own structures within the confines of the old city walls, utilizing some of the remaining architecture as ready-made stone quarries for their rebuilding efforts, while retaining the meticulously laid-out street grids of their predecessors.

There seems to be this idea circulating around the NBA that a rebuild must tear everything down to the absolute studs. That nothing should remain of the previous era. No notion. No mentality. No prolonged eye on the future.

But that's not how the Celtics or Lakers did it. And it's not how the Spurs have done it, either.

Sometimes it's okay to acknowledge the wisdom of a previous era, while knowing that it's time to turn the page. Not everything needs to be abandoned. There are some points of expertise that endure throughout the ages.

But you can't just live in the ruins, either, hoping for a lottery ticket to cure all ills, or a glorious return to form.

These Spurs aren't the Spurs of old, and that's important to acknowledge.

They're building something of their own now, but they're doing so within the thoughtfully constructed confines of a previous glory, and the result is something that feels both new and familiar.

Something as fresh as it is reminiscent. Something as aspirational as it is nostalgic.

You can't just do your laundry in the halls of a fallen kingdom. That's how you end up losing your shirt.

I have to say, Harrison Barnes has looked surprisingly spry so far this season. I assumed he would function as emergency depth when he was re-signed, but he look more like the early-season version of himself from last season, before a slump that allowed Julian Champagnie to work his way into the starting lineup. While he's certainly not a starter anymore, he's savvy and sharp-shooting enough to serve as the hot hand on nights where Carter Bryant is missing shots and assignment. That probably raises some questions about Bryant at the same time, but it really underscores just how much functional depth the Spurs have right now.

It's also been great seeing Luke Kornet find more of rhythm with the bench unit, after a somewhat concerning opening slate. There's no way the Spurs win in such a landslide without him stifling their 2nd unit, and that was his 3rd out of the last 4 games with a positive plus/minus, putting him back into the positive in Defensive Wins Shares and Defensive Box Plus/Minus for the season. I still have concerns about the postseason, but it's nice to see the trend reverse as the Spurs have badly needed it to.

And while I'm not sure that Stephon Castle's outstanding performance is indicative of how the rest of the season is going to go for him, it was an absolute blast of adrenaline to see him shoot the lights out against the Warriors specifically, especially after seeming hesitant over the past stretch of games, with the additional pain of his shot not falling. Still, you can really see why the Spurs are committed to turning him into an off-ball threat, because when that shot is falling, you become almost impossible to handle. Kudos to Mitch for having the good sense to ride the hot hand on a night when Wemby was getting a lot of defensive attention, but it also felt like this would have been a blowout even if Wemby had ridden the pine after the 1st quarter. If this was Castle finding his shot and his confidence, they really might keep trucking on at a 68-win pace. That quite literally changes everything, and bring into question whether or not rotations should even be altered all that much once Tobias Harris makes his debut, barring situational need.

Also, I'd just like to note that Keldon Johnson has really become such a patient jack-of-all for the team. It really doesn't matter who you put him with, he's going to find the point of need and do his best to fill it. There have been night where his scoring isn't needed/prioritized, and he just spent his time crashing the boards and giving it his all on defense, and nights where he comes alive on the offensive end when a particularly juicy matchup presents itself, or the team just needs more points. I'm not sure how the Spurs are going to re-sign him with their eyes on the cap and a whole host of contract balancing issues to come, but I'd love to see them do it. He's not a perfect player by any means, but he's really become a perfect Spur.

#2658. Stephen Thompson Gets Fairytale Ending to 14-Year Career With Head Kick Knockout at UFC 334

UFC 334 marked the end of Stephen Thompson's 14-year UFC career, and he couldn't have scripted a better farewell. The former two-time welterweight title challenger had already announced that his matchup against Charles Radtke would be the final fight of his career.

When fight night arrived, the 43-year-old went out in style. Thompson knocked out Radtke with his trademark spinning hook kick at 2:54 of the third round, bringing the UFC 334 prelims at Madison Square Garden to a memorable close.

Following the knockout, Thompson placed his gloves in the center of the Octagon, marking an emotional end to his time inside the cage.

The fight itself didn't start particularly well for Wonderboy. Radtke secured an early takedown in the opening minute, but Thompson eventually returned to his feet and began finding his rhythm on the feet.

ALSO READ: Merab Dvalishvili Breaks Silence After Abu Dhabi Brawl, Makes Unexpected Plea for Usman Nurmagomedov

He grew increasingly dangerous in the second round, hurting Radtke with a body kick before following up with a flurry of punches. With Thompson turning up the pressure, Radtke was forced to desperately shoot for another takedown to make it out of the round.

Thompson carried that momentum into the third, mixing up his kicks and punches while frustrating Radtke's attempts to take him down. Then came the perfect ending. Just under halfway through the round, Wonderboy unleashed a devastating spinning hook kick that sent Radtke crashing to the canvas.

It was a fitting conclusion for a karate specialist who began his UFC career with a spinning back kick knockout and chose to end it the same way. The post-fight interview with Joe Rogan was just as emotional.

Thompson took a moment to thank the fans for being part of his journey over nearly 15 years, saying, "I've been with the UFC for almost 15 years, and tonight I couldn't ask for a better way than to go out with a spinning hook kick to the dome."

Rogan, Thompson, and the American's entire team were visibly emotional after the broadcast played a video package celebrating his career. He also reflected on the power of his signature technique before thanking everyone who helped him reach the top of the sport.

He said, "I don't care if your hands are up – if you hit someone with a good old-fashioned spinning hook kick, you're going down. I told myself I wasn't going to cry. The UFC, everyone who helped get me here – my dad, my brother, my mom, my managers … but most of all, we wouldn't have this sport if it wasn't for the fans."

Thompson walks away from professional MMA with an 18-9-1 record and a legacy as one of the most recognizable strikers in UFC history. His combat sports journey, however, began long before his MMA career.

The South Carolina native started kickboxing as a teenager in 1999 before eventually transitioning to MMA in 2010. He quickly made an impression, putting together a 5-0 record and earning his UFC opportunity.

Thompson made his promotional debut at UFC 143 in February 2012 and won eight of his first nine fights. His impressive run eventually earned him two opportunities to capture the welterweight championship.

Wonderboy first challenged Tyron Woodley at UFC 205 in November 2016. Their five-round contest ended in a majority draw, setting up an immediate rematch at UFC 209 the following March. Woodley came out on top that time, retaining his title via majority decision.

Although he never managed to capture UFC gold, Thompson built an impressive resume with victories over several notable names, including Rory MacDonald, Johny Hendricks, Robert Whittaker, Jorge Masvidal, Vicente Luque, Geoff Neal, and Kevin Holland.

Now, after delivering a picture-perfect ending to his fighting career, Wonderboy can turn his attention to the next chapter of his life. The veteran also has a new role to enjoy after becoming a girl dad in September.

#2652. College football winners and losers: How the conference title game races stack up with 2 weeks to go in the 2026 season

Are we three weeks away from the last conference title games in the foreseeable college football future?

With the College Football Playoff's expansion to 24 teams becoming official on Monday, the four power conferences are doing away with their title games in 2027 as the field doubles. The status of the conference title games in the other six smaller conferences are still unknown. But there's a realistic scenario where few, if any, leagues host conference title games in 2027 and beyond.

With that in mind, here's how the races for this season's conference title games are shaping up with two weeks to go in the regular season. The Big 12, Conference USA, the Mountain West, the Pac-12 and the Sun Belt will play their title games on Friday, Dec. 5. The following day, the America, the ACC, the Big Ten, the MAC and the SEC will have their conference championships.

The Mean Green and Roadrunners are playing each other late Saturday night, while Memphis got a win on Friday night against South Florida. The Tigers have Navy and temple remaining — they're a combined 3-9 in conference play. North Texas has games against Tulane and UAB, while UTSA also gets UAB and ends the season against Tulsa. The Blazers will have a lot to say over the final two weeks.

DALLAS, TX - NOVEMBER 14: Wake Forest Demon Deacons head coach Jake Dickert talks to defensive lineman Dallas Afalava (#52) during the Atlantic Coast Conference college football game between the SMU Mustangs and the Wake Forest Demon Deacons on November 14, 2026, at Gerald J. Ford Stadium in Dallas, TX. (Photo by Matthew Visinsky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

The Hurricanes and Demon Deacons look on a collision course to meet again in the ACC title game. Miami beat Duke at home on Saturday, while Wake Forest trounced SMU to all-but eliminate the Mustangs from ACC contention. Miami beat Wake Forest 33-20 earlier in the season, but the Demon Deacons have won their last four games against ACC opponents by a combined score of 179-35.

Louisville's only hope of getting to the title game is for Wake Forest to lose its final two games of the season and to beat Pitt in Week 12.

We'll know a lot more about the Big 12 shortly, as Utah is playing at Arizona and Texas Tech is at Oklahoma State in two of the late games on Saturday night. The Wildcats and Cowboys are basically eliminated from title contention with losses.

The only way we could see a rematch of last season's title game between BYU and Texas Tech is if the Utes lose their last three games of the season.

The Bruins moved to 10-0 overall with a 22-14 win over Illinois on Friday night. If Michigan's offense showed it could do anything, then UCLA could be on a serious upset alert in Week 12. But the Wolverines have scored 13 points over their final two games after scoring a lone TD in a loss to Oregon on Saturday.

Indiana took down USC in Grant Wilson's first start at quarterback and has Washington and Purdue remaining. If the Hoosiers win out and UCLA simply goes 1-1, the Bruins will be be playing a road game in Indianapolis for the Big Ten title. If Indiana drops one of its final two games, other teams — namely, Ohio State — can get into the mix.

Everyone else in Conference USA has at least three conference losses, so this one is pretty simple. Wins by the Flames and Gamecocks in Week 12 lock in the title game matchup. The two don't meet in the regular season as Liberty has reeled off nine straight wins after a Week 1 loss to James Madison. Jacksonville State lost Saturday at Western Kentucky to snap a six-game win streak.

Miami (OH) jumped into the mix with a win over Ohio earlier in the week. With five teams in the running for the conference title game, the final two weeks of midweek MACtion should be fun. Toledo and Ohio play in the final week of the regular season, while Western Michigan and Miami (OH) play each other on the Tuesday night before Thanksgiving.

North Dakota State is rooting for New Mexico in Week 12. The Lobos visit Wyoming and a New Mexico win could put the Bison and Cowboys in a tie for second place. North Dakota State has the tiebreaker thanks to a head-to-head win. A Wyoming win, meanwhile, guarantees the Cowboys a spot in the MWC title game since their conference schedule is over after Week 12.

New Mexico lost Saturday at home to UNLV, but has a 21-16 win over North Dakota State in its pocket and plays Air Force in Week 13.

The Bobcats are emerging as the primary challengers to Boise State after wins over Oregon State and Fresno State. Boise State beat Oregon State 46-41 on Saturday night and clinched a spot in the conference title game as a result. Texas State is a game ahead of everyone else, and also lost 46-45 to Boise State just two weeks ago.

ATHENS, GA - NOVEMBER 14: Wide receiver Craig Dandridge #81 of the Georgia Bulldogs celebrates during the college football between the Missouri Tigers and the Georgia Bulldogs on November 14, 2026, at Sanford Stadium in Athens, GA. (Photo by Jeffrey Vest/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

We're down to four teams for two spots in the SEC title game. After beating Missouri on Saturday, Georgia is in the title game with a win over South Carolina in Week 12. The Gamecocks didn't have LaNorris Sellers in a loss to Arkansas on Saturday night.

If Alabama, Tennessee and Texas all finish 7-2, the Tide win the tiebreaker on conference opponent win percentage. Tennessee has the head-to-head win over Alabama and Texas has the head-to-head win over Tennessee, but Texas and Alabama didn't play each other. If there's a two-way tie between Alabama and Texas, the Tide still have the tiebreaker thanks to stronger opponents.

The Sun Belt is the only conference in college football that still has divisions. That makes it relatively easy. Louisiana Tech has already clinched the West Division. The Bulldogs are two games ahead of Louisiana and beat the Ragin' Cajuns. In the East, James Madison has the head-to-head win over Georgia Southern, but is still a game back of the Eagles. GSU has Troy in Week 12 and then plays Louisiana Tech in Week 13. JMU is off in Week 12 and has Coastal Carolina on Nov. 28.

Here are the rest of this week's winners and losers.

UConn: The Huskies took a massive step toward bowl eligibility on Saturday and can say they beat a CFP team in the process. UConn beat James Madison 46-22 thanks to three passing TDs from QB Kalieb Osborne and two rushing scores from RB Cyncir Bowers. Osborne was 16-of-20 passing for 274 yards, while Bowers rushed 25 times for 123 yards. UConn has games against Old Dominion and at Wyoming to finish the season. At 5-5, the Huskies just need a split to get a 13th game.

Kansas: Can you believe that Kansas was the first Big 12 team to really slow down West Virginia? The Jayhawks held the Mountaineers to their lowest-scoring game of the season in a 37-14 win. It wasn't turnover-induced, either. West Virginia entered Week 11 averaging 263 rushing yards per game. Saturday, WVU ran 37 times for 35 yards. QB Michael Hawkins carried the ball 25 times for 36 yards. RB Cam Cook had nine carries for 12 yards. Kansas, meanwhile, rushed 55 times for 296 yards and five scores.

Colorado: Deion Sanders has been saying for weeks that his team hadn't quit despite five losses in its last six games. Friday night's performance backed up Sanders' comments. The Buffaloes took down No. 14 Houston 42-32 thanks to 35 points over the second and third quarters. Colorado rushed 39 times for 249 yards and four different players scored rushing touchdowns. That included QB Kaneal Sweetwyne, who had to make a brief appearance thanks to Isaac Wilson's ankle injury. The Buffaloes are now 4-6, and their last two games of the season against Cincinnati and UCF suddenly look a lot more winnable.

Colorado can make a bowl game with wins in its last two games of the season.

UAB: As we mentioned above, the Blazers are in the American title game race thanks to three wins over their last four games. Saturday, UAB beat Temple 36-10 to move to 6-4 overall. The win guarantees a bowl game for UAB for the first time since 2022, when the Blazers went 7-6 under interim coach Bryant Vincent.

Texas A&M: Aggies fans who wanted Marcel Reed to be benched got their wish late in Saturday's loss to Tennessee. Brady Hart came on for Texas A&M's final possession in the 22-7 loss. However, the drive ended when Hart threw an interception himself.

That's how it's going for the Aggies this season. Reed was 9-of-22 passing for 71 yards and a pick, while Hart had two completions for 22 yards to go along with the interception. Texas A&M has lost four straight SEC games since beating Arkansas and scored 43 points across those games. Twenty of those points came against Alabama.

It's ugly in College Station as A&M is now 4-6 with games remaining at Oklahoma and against Texas. At this point, wouldn't the entire fan base trade a 5-7 season for a win over the Longhorns?

Texas A&M is now 4-6 after losing to No. 8 Tennessee. (AP Photo/Sam Craft)

Cincinnati: The Bearcats' recent performance is why Colorado will be confident when it heads to Ohio in Week 12. Cincinnati lost its third straight game on Saturday in a 41-13 drubbing at Iowa State. Cyclones RB Aiden Flora ran wild in the first half as he totaled 216 yards and scored three first-quarter touchdowns. Cincy RB Cole Tabb did what he always does with 16 carries for 165 yards, but the Bearcats' passing game was basically nonexistent and Cincinnati also went 1-for-5 on fourth downs.

NC State: It wasn't as bad as the Week 2 collapse against Vanderbilt, but NC State gave away another game Saturday. The Wolfpack lost 34-31 at home to Syracuse despite leading 31-20 with 6:55 to go and immediately getting the ball back with an Orange three-and-out.

The game flipped when CJ Bailey was intercepted by defensive lineman Tunmise Adeleye, who returned it 18 yards for the score.

Syracuse's 2-point conversion failed, but the Orange got the ball right back by forcing a three-and-out themselves. Syracuse then went on a nine-play, 49-yard drive after an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty on the punt put the Orange across midfield, and a Steve Angeli pass to Justus Ross-Simmons with 48 seconds to go was the game-winning score.

Wisconsin: The Badgers faced a Maryland team with an interim coach and a backup quarterback. They lost 24-21. Terrapins QB Cardell Williams rushed for two scores and threw for the game-winner with 2:11 to go as the Terps won their fourth game of the season. Wisconsin freshman QB Ryan Hopkins was 11-of-22 passing for 77 yards and the Badgers had just 102 yards on 31 attempts. At 6-4, Wisconsin is going bowling. But the optimism following the school's home win over USC has disappeared.

#2650. Three referees will be working in other roles on Sunday, due to the ground stop

The full scope of the adjustments to the usual officiating crews isn’t officially known. It’s clear, however, that Friday’s nationwide ground stop will result in significant changes to the usual groupings of officiating crews.

On Saturday morning, the NFL announced that three non-referees will serve as referees for four Week 10 games, with one of them — Don Willard — working as the referee for the 1:00 p.m. ET game between the Dolphins and Colts before traveling to Cincinnati for Sunday night’s Steelers-Bengals game.

Via Ben Austro of FootballZebras.com, three referees will be working in other roles on Sunday.

Referee Carl Cheffers and referee Alex Kemp will work as umpires. Referee Shawn Hochuli (pictured) will work as a back judge.

The reconfiguration resulted from the NFL’s decision to assign officials to games within driving distance of their homes.

Austro also notes that the replay officials for all Sunday games will work out of NFL headquarters. They were in Detroit on Friday for an all-day, in-person training session. Instead of fanning out to the various game locations, they all went to New York.

It sets the stage for a potentially strange day, with any mistakes inevitably being blamed on the inability of the NFL to get the officials where they needed to be. If it works, however, it could prompt the NFL to reconsider the overall staffing plan, if there’s a way to do it that reduces expenses.

I think that’s a tongue-in-cheek remark. I hope it’s a tongue-in-cheek remark.

Either way, Sunday could get interesting. The players and coaches have gotten to where they’re supposed to be. The officials haven’t, and the deck has been dramatically reshuffled in order to ensure that each game will be properly staffed.

#2647. While tied for NBA's best record, Lakers believe they can be better

While rocketing toward the top of the league, the Lakers have been far from perfect. That's good news to them.

"A big thing that we talk with our players about a lot is being able to learn and get better and try to correct things even when you are winning," coach JJ Redick said.

The Lakers (11-2) have won seven consecutive games entering Sunday's 1 p.m. PST matinee against the Suns (5-6) in Phoenix.

Using a rare multiple-day break between games to audit their performances, coaches and analytics staffers showed slide presentations to players about both offensive and defensive flaws this week. The lectures left the team with one of the best records in the league feeling as if it was one of the worst, forward Ziaire Williams joked.

Already the top-ranked offense in the league, the Lakers should strive to match that by becoming a top-10 defense, Redick implored his team. Williams is not stopping there.

"Top 10 should be at least like our standard, if not better," the forward said. "Our half-court defense has been great. Obviously, rebounding has been one of the biggest things for us, cleaning up transition as well. But the potential's there. We have the size, the length, the athleticism. It's just about going out there and executing."

Read more: Lakers' Austin Reaves considered day-to-day with heel injury

The Lakers, ranked 18th in defensive efficiency, thrive on forcing turnovers and protecting the rim. Their 18.5 turnovers forced per game rank third in the league, and they average an NBA-best 11 steals per game. Center Walker Kessler's 2.2 blocks per game rank third.

But they can't finish the strong half-court possessions. The Lakers are ranked 28th in defensive rebounding and 25th in second-chance points given up.

The Lakers staff rewatched every offensive rebound given up this season. Lack of boxing out was the biggest fault. Then there were instances when players stood and watched.

"If I stand and watch and try and outjump someone else, I'm probably not going to get the rebound," said forward Jake LaRavia, who has been an offensive rebounding revelation since entering the starting lineup, averaging 2.8 offensive rebounds in the last nine games. "So you have to go and be physical and hit bodies, and then just be able to dive on loose balls, finish possessions, it's really just who's going to work harder."

Kessler is averaging 8.1 defensive rebounds during the Lakers' seven-game winning streak — which is the second-longest in Redick's coaching tenure — compared to 6.3 during the first six games.

Forward Jarred Vanderbilt, who did not play in the first four games, has made the most of his limited minutes off the bench, grabbing 7.9 defensive rebounds per 36 minutes, the second-best rate on the team among players who have played more than three minutes. Vanderbilt, averaging 3.8 rebounds per game in 11.9 minutes, had 10 rebounds in less than 14 minutes against the Detroit Pistons on Nov. 8.

Transition defense also is sinking the Lakers' defensive efforts. Opponents are scoring 20.2 points off turnovers per game, which put the Lakers 24th out of 30 teams. Redick blames some of that on the Lakers' offensive flaws. Although they are the league's most efficient offense, the Lakers turn the ball over 16.9 times per game, the fifth-most in the NBA.

Lakers guard Luka Doncic shoots over two Bucks during a win Wednesday in Milwaukee. (Aaron Gash / Associated Press)

Luka Doncic, the league's leading scorer at 38.6 points per game, also averages an NBA-worst five turnovers. Austin Reaves, who is day-to-day because of a left heel bruise suffered Wednesday against Milwaukee, averages 24.7 points and 3.4 turnovers.

Doncic is expected to play Sunday despite tweaking his right ankle late in Wednesday's win. Reaves didn't participate in practice Saturday but Collin Sexton was a full participant. The guard wore a thick Band-Aid over his right eyebrow and had bruising around his right eye after bumping heads with Milwaukee's Ryan Rollins but said he doesn't expect to wear a mask. He needs only to keep the cut covered to ensure it doesn't open up again. The rugged guard is familiar with the protocols; Sexton said this was the 11th time in his career that he's received stitches in his face.

The short break offered an important opportunity for players to rest after a grueling three-game Eastern Conference trip. They now enter a softer stretch in the schedule. After Sunday's game in Phoenix, the Lakers play their next four at home against three teams — Charlotte, Sacramento and Utah, twice — that have a combined six wins.

Their next game against a team with a winning record isn't until Nov. 27 at San Antonio. The 11-2 Spurs, who have won 11 consecutive games, are the only team with an active winning streak longer than the Lakers'.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner marked the achievement on Instagram, sharing the team's victory post alongside three trophy emojis and a simple message: "Back to Back to Back."

Team Brady entered the E1 World Championship during its inaugural 2024 season and has now become the first outfit to win three titles in succession.

Finnish pilot Emma Kimilainen and British racer Sam Coleman have played central roles in the team's success since its arrival in the competition.

The pair helped Team Brady claim the inaugural championship before successfully defending its crown at the Miami season finale in 2025. Coleman won one of the finals while Kimilainen took the other by 15 seconds over Team Rafa's Tom Chiappe.

However, the latest title was not as straightforward. Team Brady started the 2026 campaign with a second-place finish in Jeddah before recording third place at Lake Como and runner-up finishes in Dubrovnik and Monaco.

Its breakthrough arrived at the Luanda GP in September, where Coleman won the first final before Kimilainen secured victory in the second. She held off a late challenge from Team Monaco's Oban Duncan to win by 1.4 seconds.

That result gave Team Brady a 40-point advantage over Will Smith's Westbrook Racing ahead of the Miami double-header.

The title race became tighter after Team Monaco claimed its maiden E1 victory in the first Miami round. Team Brady missed the Finals and finished last in the Race Off, allowing Westbrook Racing to cut the gap to 31 points.

Brady's team nevertheless secured the championship in the final round, completing a three-year run that has established it as the competition's first three-time consecutive champion.

The E1 World Championship offers a very different challenge from Brady's NFL career. Its all-electric RaceBird boats use hydrofoil technology to lift above the water, with each team featuring one male and one female pilot.

Brady has already won seven Super Bowls as a player. Now, his success as a team owner has added another historic achievement to his sporting career.

#2643. What placing TreVeyon Henderson on IR, activating Greg Van Roten and Reggie Gilliam means for the Patriots

At around 10 p.m. local time in Germany on Saturday, the New England Patriots announced that they have made some changes to their roster. Running back TreVeyon Henderson was headed to injured reserve due to the illness that has kept him out since late October, while fullback Reggie Gilliam and offensive lineman Greg Van Roten were both activated from IR.

With the Patriots having entered the weekend at 52 players on their roster, Saturday's transactions meant that they now have a full complement of players available again. What else do the moves mean, though? Let's find out.

TreVeyon Henderson taking to social media last Friday already was an ominous sign. In a statement addressing the illness that had kept him out for more than a week at that point, he mentioned that "my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions" were affected by the "unexpected and unusual medical emergency" he had been dealing with.

While there might still have been hope at that point that he would be able to return in a relatively short period of time, Saturday's move means that that will not be the case.

Henderson will be out for at least the next four games, starting with the upcoming contest against the Detroit Lions. Other games he is now slated to miss include matchups with the Chargers, Bills and Vikings. He is eligible to return to practice and off injured reserve ahead of the Patriots' Week 15 game in Kansas City, even though an obvious question mark hangs over that comeback given the most recent information we have available — information, head coach Mike Vrabel also did not add to this week.

"I talk to TreVeyon every day and just like everybody else that's not available, he's working hard to get back," he said on Thursday at the FC Bayern Munich training facility. "When that is I don't know. I don't have a timetable, but I love my interactions with him. I love talking with him and seeing how he's doing."

From a football perspective, Henderson going to IR officially removes the No. 2 running back from the Patriots' active roster. This leaves the group looking as follows:

53-man roster (3): Rhamondre Stevenson (38), Corey Kiner (9 | KR), Lan Larison (34)

Practice squad (1): Terrell Jennings (26)

IR (2): Myles Montgomery (39 | season-ending), TreVeyon Henderson (32)

Rhamondre Stevenson is the clear top option, something that would not change with Henderson available. He is the Patriots' most reliable back in all aspects of playing the position, and by far their best pass protector at the position. Still, Henderson as a rotational second option would bring a more dynamic element to the table than the likes of Corey Kiner and Lan Larison. That element is now missing, even though Kiner in particular has had some promising moments as of late and given Stevenson's unclear outlook — he is questionable with a knee injury — might see increased reps versus Detroit.

In addition to the roster perspective, Henderson going to IR also adds to the numbers crunch regarding the return spots. As a reminder, the Patriots had eight of those available at the start of the year but already used five on the likes of wide receivers A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins, offensive tackle Marcus Bryant and the aforementioned Reggie Gilliam and Greg Van Roten.

Two of the remaining three are expected to go to a pair of starters, wide receiver Romeo Doubs and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker. This, in turn, would potentially leave one such spot open for Henderson. Of course, if they were to qualify for the postseason, the Patriots would get two extra IR-return opportunities.

Gilliam went to injured reserve after the Patriots' Week 4 win over the Bills. He had been dealing with a knee injury entering that contest, and additionally suffered an ankle ailment in that particular game.

New England did not have a traditional fullback on the 53-man roster or practice squad at that point, and never added one either since initially losing Gilliam. This also meant that the fullback packages that were used earlier in the season were not further expanded upon, which in turn might have also played its part in the Patriots struggling to consistently move the football on the ground.

Gilliam returning will not instantly fix those issues, but he should be an immediate upgrade over the player the team primarily used to replace him, since-released rookie tight end Tanner Arkin. At the very least, the Patriots can begin incorporating those packages on a more regular and purposeful basis again.

In addition to the offensive element, Gilliam's return also might have a positive impact on the Patriots' special teams operation. His leadership has been praised repeatedly by coordinator Jeremy Springer, while he also might resume the three-unit role he played prior to his stint on IR: he was used on kickoff coverage, kickoff return and punt coverage, playing 41% of kicking game snaps over the first four weeks of the season.

The kickoff coverage element in particular will be worth watching after the Patriots have had multiple breakdowns over the last few weeks. Adding as experienced a special teamer as Gilliam to the mix might help fix those issues.

We know that the Patriots offensive line is going to look different compared to the one that started last Sunday's game against the Packers. The only question is how different.

Obviously, three spots are set in stone as they very much have been for the entire season: Will Campbell and Morgan Moses will be the starting tackles, with Jared Wilson at center. The guard positions, meanwhile, remain a revolving door.

Before looking into the options for Sunday and further into the future, let's set the scene by looking at which interior O-linemen are, and are not, available right now:

53-man roster (5): Ben Brown (77 | LG), Jared Wilson (55 | C), Matt Pryor (65 | RG), Greg Van Roten (70), Walter Rouse (72)

Practice squad (2): Xavier Newman-Johnson (64), Andrew Rupcich (67)

IR (2): Mike Onwenu (71), Alijah Vera-Tucker (75)

Ben Brown, who started last week at left guard, will not be available on Sunday against the Lions because of the knee injury he suffered in Week 9. This creates an opening Van Roten might be asked to fill, despite the fact that he played just one non-preseason snap at the position over the last seven years; the last time he played left guard extensively, Tom Brady was still the quarterback in New England.

The problem is that the alternatives are not overly attractive either, especially looking at the Lions game. Matt Pryor has limited LG experience as well, while moving him would introduce change at two spots within a unit whose success depends largely on the chemistry between its individual members. Walter Rouse, meanwhile, is questionable to play in the game after showing concussion symptoms coming out of last week's game versus the Packers.

And so, Van Roten might still be the best option after all. Long-term, however, the goal is to bring Alijah Vera-Tucker back into the mix; who will then start at right guard between Pryor, Van Roten or Brown is a question for another time.

#2639. "I feel at home”: A day in the life of RB Leipzig midfielder El Aynaoui

Moroccan international Neil El Aynaoui has started every Bundesliga and Champions League game since completing his switch from AS Roma to RB Leipzig on the deadline day on an initial loan deal. The 25-year-old midfielder shared his routines in Leipzig in the latest episode of the “Day in Life” series produced by the club.

The tour started with El Aynoaui enjoying his breakfast at home alongside his father Younes, a former top-20 ATP tennis player. He then drove his father's classic car to get to Leipzig's training center in Cottaweg, discussing his adaptation to life in Leipzig on his way to joining his teammates for a training session and recovery work.

“I used to live in the North of France. The life here (in Leipzig) is pretty the same,” the former RC Lens central midfielder said. “The team makes me feel comfortable. Every person who works at the club is honestly top. The facilities and the stadium are top.”

Leipzig coach Martin Demichelis is also new to the club, and El Aynaoui believes the Argentine has helped him to quickly adapt to the surroundings.

“The coach makes me feel at home. I also talked with him before arriving here. My teammates also make me feel at home. It's easier for me," he said.

The 25-time Moroccan international didn't want to pick a specific name when he was asked which player he has a special friendship with. “I'm gonna say the French guys. The guys who speak French."

“I actually started playing in Spain,” El Aynaoui said, revisiting his early years as a footballer.

“After I went to France, I spent most of my career at Nancy. Then I left for a bigger club in France, Lens, to play in the Champions League and first division.”

El Aynaoui made his first team debut in Ligue 2 for his hometown club before captaining them at the young age in the third tier the following season. Within a matter of months, he replaced Championnat National (the current Ligue 3) with Champions League football after a move to RC Lens.

“I played two years at Lens. It was fantastic and the club is amazing. And we're gonna face them in the Champions League this season. I'm happy to play against them,” El Aynaoui added regarding his second professional club, who are currently in a difficult state after their 9-1 home defeat to Como in the same competition already forced them to a second managerial shake-up.

“Last year, I played in Italy with Roma. And I'm now here,” El Aynaoui said at the end of going over his past clubs before speaking highly of the German mentality. “In France, we say you (Germans) are disciplined. The work rate is very important here, and I like it.”

While he spoke to RB Leipzig's media team on his way to training this time, El Aynaoui revealed that his morning routine usually involves catching up with family over the phone, emphasising the importance of staying in touch with those close to him.

After an intense training session on a sunny day, El Aynaoui completed recovery sessions in the treatment room and Leipzig's gym.

On this specific day, he took part in a tennis challenge against 2020 US Open winner Dominic Thiem after leaving the training center. His father, Younes El Aynaoui, and Maxime Estève, who also joined RB Leipzig in the summer, accompanied the duo on the tennis court.

Before preparing to end the day by watching a movie, El Aynaoui dined with his teammate Estève. “I like thrillers. My favorite movie is Shutter Island. I like a movie with a plot twist.” he said about his affection for American films.

Unlike last month, El Aynaoui will spend the international break in Leipzig as he withdrew from Morocco's squad to undergo treatment for a minor calf problem. The Atlas Lions will play against Niger in Casablanca and Rabat in their next two games in the AFCON 2027 qualifiers.

#2638. Heat Outplay Pistons For Fourth Straight Win: 3 Takeaways From Star-Studded Clash

The Miami Heat started this season 0-4, and all the alarm bells were ringing after the first few weeks of play. Slowly but surely, however, they have dug themselves out of their early hole, and now sit above .500 for the first time in the Giannis era. Tonight was a continuation of their building momentum, and perhaps one of their most impressive showings yet: a 137-117 win over the Detroit Pistons.

The Heat were in attack mode all night, likely powered by the home crowd. Two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo led the way with 34 points, 14 rebounds, eight assists, one steal, and three blocks on 76.5% shooting (1-2 from three), while center Bam Adebayo dropped 20 points, five rebounds, four assists, three steals, and two blocks on 62.5% shooting (1-2 from three). At point guard, Davion Mitchell added 15 points, four rebounds, nine assists, two steals, and two blocks on 57.1% shooting from the field (3-5 from three).

For the Pistons, star Cade Cunningham put up 33 points, five rebounds, eight assists, one steal, and one block on 40.0% shooting from the field. Off the bench, sharpshooter Kevin Huerter contributed 20 points, four rebounds, seven assists, one steal, and three blocks on 60.0% shooting (2-6 from three).

Being the second night of a back-to-back game usually means we can expect a decline in energy and focus, but that's not what we saw from Miami tonight. They came out swinging and established a nice early rhythm, eventually building a 10-point lead by the second quarter that carried them through. It was an all-around solid team performance for the Heat that shows they can compete with contenders — but what does it say about their standing in the East? In games like this, you can draw many conclusions, and here are a few that stood out after Miami's fourth-straight victory.

Four-time champion Klay Thompson was up to his usual tricks tonight, providing the Heat with a steady stream of perimeter shooting and shot-making. The longtime veteran struggled to start the season, but has recently found a spark that has contributed to Miami's streak. Tonight, Thompson had arguably one of his best games yet for the Heat, totaling 26 points, one rebound, four assists, and one block on 58.8% shooting from the field. While not quite in his prime form, Klay looks confident and rejuvenated, making it increasingly likely the Heat can continue their upward momentum.

What makes Thompson so special is that he unlocks everything for Miami by spreading the floor and creating space for Giannis. Against the Pistons, Klay's mere presence on the court pulled defenders out, and they were unable to answer whenever he delivered. Even on defense, Thompson showed flashes of his old self with bursts of speed and quick decision-making. It's an encouraging sign for Heat fans, who know how vital he is to their success.

If Klay can sustain this type of play for the rest of the season, the Heat will be in a much better position moving forward. At 36, we can't expect too much, but it's becoming clear now that Thompson still has so much more left in the tank than it appeared going in. That will surely help the Heat going forward to establish themselves as a legitimate contender in the East.

A lackluster defensive effort was arguably most to blame for the Heat's early struggles. Everyone expected them to dominate on that end, only to look completely lost for the first few weeks of play. Finally, there are signs that the defense is waking up, and it could be what powers a drastic turnaround. Tonight, they held the Pistons to just 40.2% shooting as a team while forcing 14 turnovers. They were frequently contesting shots and disrupting the offense, putting all the pressure on Cade Cunningham to bail them out.

As much as Adebayo has struggled with scoring at times, his defense remains just as effective, and it's sparking this resurgence for the Heat. In 36 minutes, he was a team-high +20 with an impressive stat line of 20 points, five rebounds, three steals, and two blocks on 62.5% shooting from the field. Behind his efforts and Giannis Antetokounmpo's interior presence, the Heat also controlled the glass, totaling 49 rebounds (to Detroit's 46).

With size, strength, and hustle at multiple positions, the Heat have all the makings of a really good defensive team, but that doesn't mean they'll figure it out right away. The good news is, they have all season to get better, and the growth has already begun.

Jalen Duren signed that massive contract extension this summer, but can the Pistons really count on him as their No. 2 guy? He's already dealing with early setbacks this season, and he was out of action again against Miami. He's only played two games all season, and his return date is still unclear. Next in line should be Ausar Thompson, but he has yet to take that leap offensively, as we saw today when he finished with just 10 points, eight rebounds, five assists, two steals, and two blocks on 62.5% shooting from the field.

On paper, Duncan Robinson has been the Pistons' second-best player this season, and that just won't cut it in the modern NBA, where teams are as stacked as ever. What happens is games like tonight, where you can focus on Cade Cunningham and essentially dare anyone else to shoot. The Pistons managed to at least make things competitive, but the lack of shot creation or playmaking outside of Cunningham put them at a disadvantage they could not overcome.

At this point, it's clear the Pistons need to find a clear, bona fide No. 2 option to take that scoring load off Cade and help the team stay afloat through an injury. Who that star might be is anyone's guess, but the Pistons should act fast to ensure that elusive title window stays wide open.

#2637. Celtics get good injury news ahead of game against Mavericks

BOSTON — The Celtics will have their full roster available when they host the Dallas Mavericks on Sunday night. Boston has no players listed on its injury report — that includes Paul George, who missed Wednesday's win over the Toronto Raptors with an illness on the second night of a back-to-back.

George sat out in Toronto just a day removed from a 36-point performance against the Philadelphia 76ers. He has been the Celtics' second-leading scorer so far this season, averaging 22 points, 5.2 rebounds, 3.8 assists, and 2.1 steals per game. He's also been the team's most efficient high-volume scorer, shooting 48.8% from the field and 44% from three.

Still, the Celtics survived without him on Wednesday, erasing a 22-point deficit on the second night of a road back-to-back to beat the Raptors 98-93. The win capped a perfect 4-0 road trip and extended Boston's winning streak to five games. At 10-2, the Celtics lead the Eastern Conference, have won 10 of their last 11 games, and own the league's best net rating.

Boston has had three days off since returning from Toronto, and now opens a home back-to-back; the Celtics host the Raptors on Sunday and then the Orlando Magic on Monday night.

Sunday's clean report doesn't guarantee the Celtics will be at full strength on both nights. Boston has rested players on back-to-backs before this season: Mitchell Robinson sat the front end in Orlando on Nov. 1, and George sat the second night in Houston the following day.

Jayson Tatum, meanwhile, has played in every back-to-back game so far, though he's said he's open to conversations about rest management. He also noted that he doesn't like sitting out road games, which has factored into his decision to play on the second night of multiple back-to-backs.

"It's my 10th year, so I understand the balance of wanting to play every game, and rest, and back-to-backs, three-in-fours, five-in-sevens," Tatum said last week in Charlotte. "It's always a conversation. We talk about it. We have a plan. I don't really like sitting out on away games, but we just kind of figure it out as we go."

The Celtics will begin a four-game West Coast road trip on Wednesday, which includes stops in Denver, Sacramento, San Francisco, and Washington D.C.

Dallas will arrive in Boston after facing the Cleveland Cavaliers on Saturday night; the Mavericks entered that game at 7-5 after getting blown out by the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving were both off Dallas' injury report for Saturday's game.

Flagg, the reigning Rookie of the Year, is averaging 24.6 points, 6.9 rebounds, and 6.5 assists per game, while Irving is scoring 21.6 points per game. Irving, who returned this season from a torn ACL, sat out the second night of Dallas' first back-to-back of the season for load management, so it's possible he misses Sunday's game, though the Mavericks have yet to list their injury report.

Max Christie (left ankle sprain), Sergio De Larrea (right knee sprain), Tarik Biberović (right heel bursitis), and Dereck Lively II (right foot surgery recovery) were all ruled out ahead of Saturday's game.

Sunday will be Flagg's second game at TD Garden. The Newport, Maine native drew plenty of support from the crowd during his Garden debut last March; the Celtics won the game by 20 as Jayson Tatum made his return from his Achilles injury.

Celtics-Mavericks tips off on Sunday night at 6pm ET.
